items.title: A Surrogate Boundary Condition for Improved Accuracy and Performance of Local Modeling in Radiation Transport Simulations
items.summary: Monte Carlo neutronics analysis of tokamak designs is computationally expensive due to the complex CAD geometries required to accurately model them. Design iteration of port plugs using global transport in the full model is impractical because of the computational cost. To circumvent this, local modeling methods are used. In the local modeling method, a boundary condition is assumed on the port plug, such that particles that leave the port plug do not require transport in the surrounding global model. For this purpose, vacuum and reflective boundaries are assumed, both of which provide poor approximation of the true transport physics in the global model. To improve on current techniques, a surrogate model is presented that provides a physics-informed boundary condition for the component. A neural network is trained to reproduce the boundary condition on the component that represents the behavior of particles returning from the surrounding geometry. Monte Carlo transport is only necessary within the component, and approximate physics from the surrounding region are retained. This approach allows the design in the component to be iterated without requiring full model transport and joining of the component mesh to the global mesh in each iteration. In this work, the surrogate model is evaluated against vacuum and reflective boundaries-- outperforming both in accuracy, with surrogate predictions of the flux in the port plug differing less than 12% from the global transport solution in any given energy bin. The surrogate boundary condition is also demonstrated to be more performant than global transport for the simplified benchmark geometry.

items.title: KELP v1.0: an agent-ready Lagrangian particle tracker for unstructured meshes and HEALPix grids
items.summary: Lagrangian particle tracking follows virtual particles in the velocity fields of an ocean model to study transport pathways, connectivity and dispersion. Setting up such a study takes many technical steps, and this work is increasingly done with coding agents, programs in which a language model writes code, runs it and checks the result. We present KELP v1.0, the Kinematic Engine for Lagrangian Particles, a tracker for unstructured ocean-model meshes and HEALPix grids that is built to be operated by such agents. KELP computes two- and three-dimensional trajectories with established methods on triangular, quadrilateral and mixed meshes, with global FESOM2 and coastal FESOM-C meshes as examples, and on HEALPix, the equal-area grid on which kilometre-scale digital twins distribute their output. Documentation and short task instructions, called skills, tell an agent how to prepare releases and configurations, run calculations and process the trajectories. An agent prepared and ran all experiments of this paper with these skills, and most of the preparation was completed within hours. In a controlled evaluation, the skills raised the completeness of study files prepared by five language models from 75-93% to 88-100%. KELP reproduced the particle distributions of two other trackers on the same fields. Trajectories on HEALPix fields converged to those on the model mesh as the pixels were refined. After one year, the median distance between the two was 1.6 km at a pixel spacing of 25.5 km. HEALPix output can therefore be used for Lagrangian studies of ensemble statistics when the original mesh is not available. In a 63-year calculation with 7.92 million particles released in the Beaufort Gyre, transport from the gyre to Fram Strait took years to decades, and the run took 3 h 36 min on one 128-core node. A test tracked $10^{10}$ particles on a HEALPix mesh of 35.5 million wet surface nodes.

items.title: Complex fluid flow dynamics by bright scattershot boson sampling
items.summary: Boson sampling machines have become a fruitful tool for establishing new concepts, which connect fundamental physics with computer science applications. Here, we exploit the intrinsically high-dimensional correlations generated by the measurement outcomes of a multiphoton boson sampling machine and demonstrate how a reconfigurable architecture can be programmed to autonomously model the time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems that describe complex fluid flows. By extending on the original scattershot boson sampling (SBS) scheme to include higher photon number components -- a scheme which we label bright scattershot boson sampling (BSBS) --- this scheme overcomes scaling issues inherent to SBS-based schemes by utilizing all randomly generated input photon number distributions. We illustrate the capability of this scheme for two complex fluid-flow models: an eight-dimensional Lorenz-type model of two-dimensional thermally driven convection and a 16-dimensional model of global atmospheric circulation. Using a digital twin of the BSBS architecture based on multiphoton statistics, we show that the photonic approach accurately reproduces the temporal dynamics of both systems while being resilient to photon losses of up to 50 per cent. We also verified that the BSBS case outperforms a comparable run with coherent light. Moreover, its prediction horizon exceeds that of a classical reservoir-computing model with the same query complexity. These results highlight the potential of near-term photonic quantum computing for addressing relevant real-world tasks on noisy intermediate-scale devices.

items.title: Restoring Consistency with Poynting's Theorem in Numerical MHD and RMHD
items.summary: For perfectly conducting plasmas, Poynting's theorem states that the time rate of change of electromagnetic energy density equals the negative of the divergence of the Poynting flux. To the best of our knowledge, this involutive theorem has never been mimetically incorporated in codes. We show that there is an inconsistency in MHD and RMHD codes that evolve face-centered magnetic fields in globally-divergence-free fashion. This is because the face-centered flux of energy density, which incorporates a Poynting vector, is evaluated using one-dimensional Riemann solvers that are applied at face-centers. However, the face-centered magnetic fields are evolved according to edge-centered electric fields that come from two-dimensional Riemann solvers that are applied to the edges of a zone. While edge-centered electric fields are used to evolve the magnetic field, they have no influence on the face-centered Poynting flux. For situations where the magnetic energy is much larger than the thermal energy, this causes a negative pressure to be evaluated at the zone-centers. This paper restores consistency by using edge-centered variables to evaluate a face-centered Poynting flux. A simple accuracy-preserving correction is made to the face-centered flux of energy density. We show that it helps considerably in simulations that have very strong magnetic fields.

items.title: Solution of the Qubit Marginal Problem from Fermionic Representability
items.summary: Whether local reduced states are compatible with a global quantum state---the quantum marginal problem---is central to quantum information and simulation. Here we present a solution to the ensemble marginal problem for qubits based on the representability theory of fermions. Encoding each qubit as one fermion in two orbitals, we prove that the representable qubit marginals form an exposed face of the set of $N$-representable fermionic reduced density matrices, selected by the vanishing of every site-occupation variance. Complete hierarchies of fermionic representability conditions therefore transfer exactly to qubits. Applications to frustrated Heisenberg and transverse-field Ising rings show that the $(2,3)$-positivity conditions are exact at the Majumdar--Ghosh point and accurate to about 0.5% at criticality. Because the conditions hold for any quantum state, they also provide a framework for mitigating measurement errors on qubit-based quantum devices.

items.title: Verifying the High-Energy Tail in Bi-Kappa Particle Loading: Three-Dimensional Tests, Velocity Bounds, and Finite Precision
items.summary: The bi-Kappa distribution models anisotropic space-plasma populations with suprathermal power-law tails. Kinetic simulations represent such a population by computational particles, and a loader draws their velocities from the requested bi-Kappa distribution, which we call the target distribution. When $κ$ is close to 1/2, floating-point underflow can remove the largest draws, and a velocity bound changes the loaded distribution. Published Kappa loaders are usually verified by comparing histograms of the speed or of one velocity component with the analytic distribution. Such comparisons do not examine the direction of the velocity or whether the direction is independent of the speed. We build an anisotropic loader on an established Gamma-ratio construction and examine each of these problems. Near $κ=1/2$, evaluating the Gamma ratio on a logarithmic scale avoids the loss of draws to underflow in single and double precision down to $κ=0.5001$. When draws outside a bound on each velocity component are discarded and redrawn, a small rejected fraction can accompany a large change in the tail. At $κ=2$ and $θ_\parallel=2θ_\perp$, a bound at 20 times each component's thermal speed rejects a fraction $3.6\times10^{-4}$ of the draws and lowers the 99.9th-percentile speed by 11%. We test the loaded velocities through their direction and their normalized radius, the length of the velocity after each component is divided by $\sqrtκ$ times its thermal speed. The tests used nine values of $κ$ from 0.51 to 10, including $1/2<κ\le3/2$, where the second moments do not exist, with $θ_\parallel=2θ_\perp$ in double precision. At every $κ$, $χ^2$ tests find the normalized radius out to its 99.999th percentile, the direction, and their joint distribution consistent with the target distribution.

items.title: An Invariant Neural-Network Eddy-Viscosity Closure with Iterative Solver Coupling for Molten Salt Fast Reactor Thermal-Hydraulics
items.summary: System thermal-hydraulics codes such as the System Analysis Module (SAM) close turbulence on coarse meshes with algebraic zero-equation mixing-length models. These models cannot represent the non-equilibrium turbulence, flow separation, and large-scale recirculation of open-cavity advanced reactors. We develop an invariant neural-network eddy-viscosity closure for SAM and apply it to the Molten Salt Fast Reactor (MSFR). The closure predicts the turbulent kinetic energy and timescale of each element from the flow and geometry of its neighbors, without solving turbulence transport equations. The resulting non-negative eddy viscosity enters the implicit diffusive operator, which keeps the momentum equations well conditioned. We prove that the closure is exactly invariant to translation, Galilean boost, rotation, reflection, and neighbor ordering. A network trained on high-order Nek5000 fields sees a different feature distribution on the coarse SAM mesh. We remove this covariate shift by iteratively retraining the network on SAM flow states against fixed Nek5000 targets. For a held-out steady state, the coupled closure reproduces the single recirculation cell and eddy-viscosity plume of the Nek5000 reference. In a 120 s pump-coastdown transient, it halves the velocity error of the mixing-length model, from 37.6% to 17.7%, and matches the Nek5000 eddy viscosity with a time-averaged relative error of 12%. The remaining velocity error comes from the coarse mesh. The coupled transient takes about 0.2 core-hours, compared with about 330 core-hours for Nek5000. The results show that the closure can recover two-equation RANS turbulence behavior in a coarse-mesh system code at a small fraction of the CFD cost.

items.title: Blind in-memory arithmetic with confined skyrmions: doubling and successor functions on a skyrmion byte
items.summary: We present a skyrmionic-based computation platform, able to perform fully in-memory computing by collectively manipulating the skyrmions that serve as bits of the binary memory. The computation protocols are implemented through driving currents and adequately located anisotropy defects that modify the dynamics of the skyrmions along a magnetic track. Simulations demonstrating the feasibility of such an in-memory computing system are shown for several basic and simple mathematical operations with natural numbers, such as doubling and adding one (the successor function). We also discuss how further optimization of the geometry, barrier profiles, current amplitudes, and timing parameters could improve both the robustness and the overall practical feasibility of the system.

items.title: Fine-tuned atomistic foundation model for accurate sodium-carbon chemistry in Na-ion batteries
items.summary: Atomistic foundation models have emerged as a promising route to DFT-level accuracy for materials simulation with complex chemical environments. However, their reliability across competing bonding regimes and, more importantly, how complex bonding affects predictions of material properties remain unclear. Among materials with competing bonding regimes, sodium storage in hard carbon poses a substantial challenge. Hard carbon features diverse local structural motifs, including defective and curved graphitic regions, amorphous regions, and closed/open pores. Motivated by its importance for Na-ion batteries, we systematically evaluate existing pretrained foundation models based on the MACE architecture across different local Na/C motifs. We find that the pretrained models fail to accurately capture Na-Na and Na-C interactions for metallic Na clusters on graphene. To recover a DFT-level energetic description, we employ targeted fine-tuning, showing that it can describe the energetic stability of local motifs and achieve sufficient transferability to unseen Na/C environments. With the developed fine-tuned model, we establish a correlation between closed-pore radius in hard carbon and plateau voltage, showing that the small pores contribute at larger voltages than large ones, suggesting thus how the developed fine-tuned foundation model can link atomistic information with materials design for complex bonding environments.

items.title: A charge-dependent electron emission yield from electron irradiated dielectrics
items.summary: The total electron emission yield (TEEY) of dielectric surfaces may vary during electron irradiation owing to charge accumulation within the material. In the present work, the generation, transport, and escape formulation of Dionne is extended by introducing an additional attenuation of secondary electrons that depends on trapped positive charge. The resulting emission law is coupled to a charge-balance equation, allowing the TEEY to be calculated as a function of incident energy and injected charge. The model is examined using measurements on polycrystalline Al2O3, from which effective cross sections describing interactions between trapped charge and secondary electrons are determined. Their mean value is then used to predict the evolution of the TEEY curves without further adjustment. Finally, an analytical approximation of the nonlinear charging law is derived to facilitate the implementation in electron-irradiation simulations.

items.title: Intrinsic Wannier Functions for Hamiltonian downfolding
items.summary: Downfolding ab initio material band structure into a low-energy subspace spanned by orbitals of specified atomic character, a procedure known as Wannier downfolding, is a common task in the simulation of complex materials. We introduce the Intrinsic Wannier Function (IWF) method to Wannierize bands with given atomic character. The method is non-iterative and requires only a single dimensionless parameter to disentangle bands. In benchmarks on silicon, graphene, and the three-band model of a mercury cuprate, we show that Intrinsic Wannier Functions provide high quality downfolded band structures compared to those from standard approaches such as Maximally Localized Wannier Functions, the Selected Columns of the Density Matrix method, and Projectability-Disentangled Wannier Functions. Further, their straightforward implementation and robustness position Intrinsic Wannier Functions as a general and useful tool for Wannier downfolding in materials electronic structure and in high-throughput applications.

items.title: Evidence-Guided Neural Architecture Selection under Uncertainty for Subject-Specific Blood Glucose Forecasting
items.summary: Reliable neural architecture selection is an open challenge in time-series forecasting under limited, noisy, and heterogeneous data, where standard heuristic architecture design and validation approaches fail to ensure accurate and reliable prediction and generalization. We propose EVIDENT (EVidence-based IDEntification of Neural archiTectures), a framework for architecture selection that integrates Bayesian training, evidence-based ranking, and task-specific validation under uncertainty. The framework explores the candidate architecture pool and identifies the lowest-capacity model that satisfies a prescribed validation criterion. We demonstrate this method using temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) for individualized blood glucose forecasting in type 1 diabetes patients. The results show that EVIDENT systematically rejects both under- and over-parameterized TCN architectures on population-level diabetes data, while identifying models that generalize reliably to unseen patients. When multiple architectures are competitive, the framework further supports plausibility-weighted ensemble predictions that enhance predictive performance. Compared with a random-search baseline, EVIDENT identified smaller architectures with more consistent forecasting performance on unseen patients. These findings establish EVIDENT as a strategy to neural architecture discovery, enabling reliable model selection for high-consequence forecasting in data-limited and heterogeneous settings.

items.title: The effect of particle shape on sunlight exposure in a wind-driven free-surface flow
items.summary: We investigate how nonspherical marine particles, such as microplastics, phytoplankton, and ice, are exposed to sunlight near the water surface in wind-driven surface boundary layer conditions. We measure the depth and orientation of these particles in a laboratory wind-wave tank, then use this data to model how much sunlight the particles would be exposed to in an aquatic environment. In particular, we explore how their orientation affects their sunlight exposure in these conditions, since most studies to date do not account for orientation, turbulent shear flow, and wind-waves at the water surface. We find that in all cases, particles prefer certain orientations, and this causes the average sunlight exposure of the particles to be 5 to 40\% higher than would be expected if their orientations were random. Further, we find that the mean irradiance depends on the ratio of the particle mixing length $L_m$ to the light decay lengthscale $λ$, and the nature of this dependence differs between disks and rods. Disks experience disproportionately greater mean irradiance at smaller $L_m/λ$ due to the vertical variation in their orientations. These results have important implications for accurately estimating the sunlight exposure of particles in the surface boundary layer.

items.title: Topological phase diagram of an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with negative coupling
items.summary: Recently, an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with three atoms per unit cell has been experimentally realized in perovskite exciton-polariton micropillars. A distinctive feature of this system is that the second and third bands undergo a topological transition through a band crossing at the wave vector $k=0$, associated with a negative coupling. In this work, we analytically determine the phase diagram of the model as a function of the on-site energy splitting and the ratio of intercell to intracell hopping amplitudes. We identify seven regions in this lane, with four distinct topological phases, characterized by different Zak phases of the three bands. Our results provide a useful theoretical framework for interpreting existing experiments and serve as a guide for future experimental investigations of this system.

items.title: Tunable Hybridization of Whispering Gallery Modes in High-Index Photonic Molecules
items.summary: Photonic molecules formed by coupled dielectric microresonators provide a platform for controlling collective optical modes, yet the interplay between molecular topology, resonator detuning, and dielectric environment in determining their spectral response remains insufficiently quantified. Here, we systematically quantify the evolution of Whispering Gallery Mode (WGM) hybridization in high-index TiO$_2$ and perovskite coated TiO$_2$ microresonators with molecular topology, and establish the corresponding effective inter-cavity coupling using a combined numerical and analytical analysis. We further show that perovskite-shell incorporation provides a diameter and thickness-dependent modification of the effective coupling, producing a non-monotonic response rather than a uniform suppression of coupling. Despite the resulting closely spaced hybridized resonances in the high-index perovskite environment, the supermodes remain spectrally resolvable, with $Q$-factor of order \(10^3\) for representative modes. The observed spectral splitting is quantitatively related to the effective inter-cavity coupling strengths, revealing a non-monotonic coupling response to perovskite-shell incorporation that depends on resonator size and shell thickness. These results establish molecular topology and dielectric environment as distinct parameters for controlling WGM hybridization, inter-cavity coupling, and spectral response, providing a basis for the design of coupled resonator systems for applications in optical sensing, filtering, switching, and other resonant photonic devices.

items.title: Generation of low-frequency flows by shear Alfvén waves in magnetohydrodynamics
items.summary: Coherently forced, weak reduced-magnetohydrodynamic turbulence is studied in a uniform plasma to investigate the long-term nonlinear interactions of shear Alfvén waves. The 'pump waves' are chosen to model toroidal Alfvén eigenmodes, excited by suprathermal particles in magnetic fusion devices. Modes with zero frequency and no variation along the magnetic field are generated nonlinearly; these produce analogues of zonal flows and currents in a gradient-free system. This indicates that quasistationary flows can be generated by shear Alfvén waves in systems simpler than those previously considered, which relied on compressibility, finite-Larmor-radius effects, or complex geometry. The saturated amplitudes of the modes are found analytically and numerically as a function of pump-wave amplitude. This facilitates estimates of the critical amplitude above which toroidal Alfvén eigenmodes can generate sufficiently strong zonal flows to suppress microturbulence in the core of magnetic fusion devices. This threshold corresponds to magnetic fluctuations whose amplitude, relative to the background field, is comparable to $ρ_{\star i}$, the ion Larmor radius normalised to the minor radius of the device.

items.title: Graph diffusion transformer for interpretable generation and inverse design of disordered atomic structures
items.summary: Atomic disorder offers a potent degree of freedom to tailor material properties, yet the resulting vast configuration space obscures structure-property relations and hinders rational inverse design. Here we introduce Graph Amorphous Diffusion Transformer (GaDiT), a generative model that combines dynamic periodic graphs, masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution. GaDiT generates high-quality disordered structures while accelerating sampling by two orders of magnitude compared with existing corrector-based approaches, as demonstrated across two-dimensional amorphous carbon and three-dimensional amorphous silicon and silica. Moreover, GaDiT supports conditional generation under single or combined structural features, physical properties and preparation conditions in a unified model, and enables inverse design that expands accessible structure-property ranges beyond the training distribution. To interpret these structures and the trained network, we propose a conditioned atomic response mapping analysis, revealing both the global structural descriptors and the local atomic environments that govern target properties. Overall, GaDiT establishes a general framework for interpretable generation, inverse design and structure-property discovery for disordered atomic structures.

items.title: Number fluctuations and particle loss in Dicke superradiance
items.summary: Dicke superradiance, the collective spontaneous emission of identical quantum emitters into a common reservoir, produces a burst with a characteristic delay $t_{\mathrm{SR}}$ and a peak intensity that scales quadratically with the emitter number $N$. This strong dependence makes the burst sensitive to how many emitters actually participate. In experiments, however, this number is rarely fixed: it fluctuates between preparations and decreases during emission through atom loss. Here we extend the analytical treatment of superradiance to variable emitter numbers using the Schwinger-boson mapping of the collective spin onto two bosonic modes. In this formulation, collective decay annihilates an atom in the excited-state mode and creates one in the ground-state mode. We find that number fluctuations enhance emission and that the ensemble-averaged emission trace encodes the initial number distribution. We show how to reconstruct second-order correlations from photon counting with finite detection efficiency and temporal resolution, even when the full distribution cannot be resolved. For atom loss at rate $r$, we derive exact results for the population dynamics and show that the peak intensity scaling is governed by the single scaling variable $g_{\mathrm{r}}=r t_{\mathrm{SR}}$. The peak remains quadratic in $N$ for $g_{\mathrm{r}}<1$, follows logarithmically corrected subquadratic power laws for $g_{\mathrm{r}}>1$, and crosses over to linear scaling under strong loss with $g_{\mathrm{r}}\gg1$.

items.title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs
items.summary: Research in the domain of Physics-Informed Neural Networks applied to PDE modelling has advanced significantly in recent years, providing a wide ecosystem of novel methods. However, one frequent limitation is the inability of PINNs to scale out on High-Performance Computing architectures to address more ambitious challenges, particularly non-linear physics models with turbulent dynamics in large spatial domains. Typical studies restrain demonstrations to toy models with simple physics equations, few variables, and rarely any complex non-linear dynamics evolved over long timescales. Part of the AI community has even adopted the idea that "PINNs don't scale". This work proves otherwise. We present a mathematically robust formulation of Finite-Element-Method for Neural Networks (FEM-NN) implemented into a comprehensive, modular framework: Fuse-PINN. This formulation provides the basis for a sclable parallelisation of Physics-Informed Neural Networks on GPU-based HPC systems. Furthermore, an Energy Natural Gradient Descent optimiser is implemented to allow high-precision convergence. Fuse-PINN is demonstrated on physics models relevant to Magnetic Confinement Fusion, including non-linear convective models with fine-scale dynamics. Near-perfect scaling is achieved on multi-GPU runs with increasing problem size.

items.title: Macroscopic Nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer Mediated by Coherent Magnons
items.summary: Phonon-mediated nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer (RET) in metal deuterides is severely constrained by inertial rest-mass dilution, lattice fracture limits, and thermal nuclear spin cancellation. Extending the generalized nuclear Dicke model to Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) magnons eliminates mass dilution via hyperfine-amplified M1 coupling while unlocking relativistic Dirac M2 coupling via Overhauser spin polarization. We derive a Suhl-clamped FMR scaling law predicting 14.2 MeV (Pd-106) and 11.4 MeV (Ni-58) breakup neutrons, 19.9 MeV alpha particles, and reconciled sub-keV fusion anomalies.

items.title: Experimenters' Free Will and Quantum Certainty
items.summary: Physics has long lived with a split personality that desires determinism for measured systems while demanding that experimenters decide what to measure on a whim. Intriguingly, such a free will assumption for experimenters has thwarted many attempts to provide a satisfactory explanation of how quantum probabilities evolve to clear-cut measurements. An overview of this quantum measurement problem is presented without equations, and the lesson is drawn that denial of experimenters' free will may be the only workable solution. A holistic view is offered of a self-consistent superdetermined spacetime block universe of events. The goal of future research is to develop the underlying principle that generates this Escher-like global pattern.

items.title: Coupled stochastic variational principles for multiscale surface gravity waves -- Part I: theoretical framework
items.summary: This paper develops a comprehensive stochastic variational framework for surface gravity waves. Starting from Luke's variational principle for irrotational, incompressible free-surface flow, we introduce a decomposition of the velocity potential into a large-scale deterministic component and a regularized stochastic noise term representing unresolved scales. A path-wise variational principle yields the stochastic counterparts of the Laplace, Bernoulli, and kinematic boundary conditions. To close the system, a second variational principle in expectation is formulated, providing evolution equations for the noise correlation functions. The resulting coupled system preserves the Hamiltonian structure of the Zakharov--Craig--Sulem formulation. We further analyze explicit solutions via WKB approximation and show that the noise correlation functions satisfy a Hamilton-Jacobi equation with ray-tracing dynamics. This framework provides a rigorous foundation for reduced stochastic models of ocean waves and for the kinetic theory developed in the companion paper.

items.title: A fast and rigorous numerical tool to measure length-scale artifacts in molecular simulations
items.summary: The two-sided Bogoliubov inequality for classical and quantum many-body systems is a theorem that provides rigorous bounds on the free-energy cost of partitioning a given system into two or more independent subsystems. This theorem motivates the definition of a quality factor which directly quantifies the degree of statistical-mechanical consistency achieved by a given simulation box size. A major technical merit of the theorem is that, for systems with two-body interactions and a known radial distribution function, the quality factor can be computed by evaluating just three six-dimensional integrals. We present a numerical algorithm for computing the quality factor and demonstrate its consistency with respect to results in the literature obtained from simulations performed at different box sizes.

items.title: Match classification in the last round of four-team round-robin tournaments
items.summary: Classification of matches played in the last rounds of sports competitions is a well-established tool for evaluating tournament designs. Our paper offers the first comparison of deterministic and probabilistic match classification models by analysing the most prominent example of four-team round-robin competitions, the group stage of the FIFA World Cup. We show that both models are highly relevant in practice: all (four) deterministic and (six) probabilistic match types occurred in the 2014 and 2018 FIFA World Cups, respectively. The probabilistic model, which accounts for the relative benefits of attacking and defending, provides a deeper insight; for instance, the competitive matches from the deterministic approach can be of any of the six probabilistic types. Therefore, the probabilistic model is used to decompose the impact of three reforms introduced in the 2026 FIFA World Cup: the expansion to 48 teams, the modified qualification rules, and head-to-head tie-breakers.

items.title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
items.summary: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.

items.title: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for kinetic shock waves: simultaneous accuracy of lower- and higher-order moments, with and without moment supervision
items.summary: We investigate physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for one-dimensional kinetic shock waves governed by the Bhatnagar--Gross--Krook (BGK) and Shakhov collision models, with and without moment supervision. The trace-free third-order and the fourth-order moments enter the fluxes of stress and heat flux through a shock; the aim, to our knowledge not previously examined for kinetic PINNs, is simultaneous accuracy of these and the lower-order moments of one predicted distribution. Data-assisted calculations, including anchor and closure studies, combine kinetic residuals with moment observations. For the BGK shock tube, a positive eight-moment representation whose spatial envelope follows the far-field decay of the initial condition gives heat-flux, stress and higher-moment discrepancies of $0.33\%$, $0.67\%$ and $1.8$--$2.0\%$ against the 6400-cell discrete-velocity method (DVM) reference supplying its observations; a five-field representation leaves the latter uncontrolled. Equation-trained characteristic-integral PINNs use analytic initial and incoming-boundary distributions and their own predicted moments. Their BGK and Shakhov shock-tube heat-flux and stress discrepancies are $0.41\%$ and $0.36\%$ against 3200-cell references; against the 6400-cell reference the BGK values are $0.21\%$ and $0.18\%$, and $0.4$--$0.9\%$ for the higher moments. Stationary neural continuation covers Shakhov Mach 2--5 and BGK Mach 6--7. Characteristic correction reduces the Mach-7 heat-flux and stress discrepancies from $3.37\%$ and $1.34\%$ to $0.42\%$ and $0.43\%$; at Mach~8 they are $0.62\%$ and $0.79\%$, and at Mach~12, across references, $0.40$--$1.03\%$ and $0.41$--$2.65\%$. Three independent Mach-2 initialisations assess repeatability. It is established that lower moments do not determine higher ones; the contribution is to quantify which moments each information regime recovers.

items.title: A systematic comparison of physics-informed neural networks and mechanistic models for epidemic modeling and forecasting
items.summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently been applied to epidemic modeling and forecasting with promising results. These methods integrate mechanistic knowledge with data-driven learning. Yet, their comparative performance against well-established, and simpler epidemic models is underexplored. Here, we conduct a systematic comparison of a PINN-based framework and a stochastic mechanistic model. Both approaches share the same age-structured SEIRD core and rolling-window forecasting pipeline, in a deliberately minimal setting. We evaluate their retrospective fits and probabilistic forecasts in two synthetic scenarios and the first COVID-19 wave in London. Interestingly, while PINNs underperform in synthetic scenarios, they achieve better performance on real data. Furthermore, PINNs provide narrower uncertainty intervals and sharper estimation of parameters in synthetic scenarios. Our findings confirm PINNs as a promising tool in epidemiology. At the same time, the results reaffirm the value of simpler approaches such as traditional compartmental models, and promote additional benchmarking studies.

items.title: Enhanced Hyperspectral Nano-FTIR Imaging by Neural-Network-Based Processing of Multiple Signal Harmonics
items.summary: Nano-FTIR spectroscopy combines infrared spectroscopy with nanometer-scale spatial resolution and enables hyperspectral nanoimaging. However, quantitative measurements typically rely on higher-harmonic near-field signals, which are largely background-free but suffer from low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Lower harmonics provide substantially higher SNR but contain significant background contributions that distort the near-field response and hinder quantitative analysis. Here, we introduce a cross-harmonic neural network (CHNN) that exploits the complementary information encoded in multiple harmonic channels to denoise third-harmonic hyperspectral data. Trained directly on experimental nano-FTIR datasets, the CHNN uses first- and second-harmonic spectra to improve the SNR of the third-harmonic response. Applied to a PMMA/PS polymer blend, it substantially reduces noise while preserving spectral features and nanoscale spatial contrast. Compared with conventional single-harmonic denoising using an autoencoder, the CHNN achieves superior noise suppression. These results demonstrate the potential of lower-harmonic signals for improving hyperspectral nano-FTIR imaging without increasing acquisition time.

items.title: Learning transferable event representations for charmed baryon physics at BESIII
items.summary: Deep learning has become an essential tool in high-energy physics, where the ability to learn transferable event representations can significantly improve model generalization across related physics processes. In this work, we present a Particle Transformer-based framework for learning such representations for charmed baryon physics in the BESIII experiment. The framework is implemented through large-scale pre-training on Monte Carlo simulation samples and subsequent fine-tuning for downstream analyses. Using the production and decays of the charmed baryon $Λ_c^+$ as a benchmark, we develop pre-trained models for both event classification and momentum-direction regression. The classification model learns discriminative event representations for the dominant physics categories, rejecting $96.90\%$ of background events at a signal efficiency of 90.00\%. Across 12 benchmark $Λ_c^+$ decay channels, fine-tuning from the pre-trained model achieves performance comparable to or better than training from scratch, with particularly clear improvements in low-statistics regimes. For the regression task, the pre-trained model improves the average angular resolutions across the same benchmark channels. Further improvement is obtained after fine-tuning in the representative semileptonic decay $Λ_c^+ \to p K^- e^+ ν_e$. In addition, the predicted momentum direction enables reconstruction of the parent kinematics without a recoil-side tag and thereby increases signal efficiency. For this semileptonic decay, the pre-trained regression model increases the signal efficiency by approximately one order of magnitude relative to the double-tag method. This strategy provides a scalable solution for a wide range of physics cases at BESIII and can be extended to other high energy experiments.

items.title: Adjoint-State Identifiability of Piezo-Tunable Valley Splitting in 2D Magnetic Heterostructures
items.summary: Mechanical strain has been proposed to dynamically tune proximity-induced valley splitting in 2D magnetic heterostructures for solid-state information processing. While first-principles studies routinely predict strain-modulated valley splittings at the atomic scale, they rarely address whether the coupling parameter can be extracted from a macroscopic transport measurement against realistic device noise. This paper develops a classical, partial differential equation-constrained multiscale inverse framework to quantify the device-level identifiability of the exchange-strain coupling from a transverse Hall voltage in a molybdenum disulfide and chromium tribromide heterostructure. Structural relaxation confirms a chiral $C_3$ point-group symmetry of the Hollow-stacked structure, and Neumann's principle reduces the coupling tensor to a single scalar $η$. Dispersion-corrected density functional theory gives a zero-strain splitting of -0.45 meV and bounds the coupling to $|η| \lesssim 2$ meV at small tensile strain while leaving its sign open, motivating the transport analysis. For an example coupling of $|η| = 0.56$ meV, where an actuator strain trace of $3.5 \times 10^{-4}$ shifts the valley splitting by only 0.2 $μ$eV, operation at 10 K below the Curie temperature of CrBr$_3$ makes the coupling statistically resolvable from 5.6 to 3,704 V/cm. Even in a demanding stress test recovering $η$ jointly with the zero-strain splitting, an uncalibrated Hall gain, and an unknown intervalley scattering time, the window spans 25 to 3,704 V/cm and the Cramér-Rao bound at the 10% velocity-saturation limit reaches 13.6 $μ$eV, 21 times below the resolution criterion. Since this window covers the full operational bias range of 2D field-effect transistors, from low-power linear readout to high-field drive, this framework serves as a pre-fabrication diagnostic for valleytronic devices.

items.title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
items.summary: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.

items.title: Catenaries in viscous fluid
items.summary: This work explores a simple model of a slender, flexible structure in a uniform flow, providing analytical solutions for the translating, axially flowing equilibria of strings subjected to a uniform body force and drag forces linear in the velocities. The classical catenaries are extended to a five-parameter family of curves. A sixth parameter affects the tension in the curves. Generic configurations are planar, represented by a single first order equation for the tangential angle. The effects of varying parameters on representative shapes, orbits in angle-curvature space, and stress distributions are shown. As limiting cases, the solutions include configurations corresponding to "lariat chains" and the towing, reeling, and sedimentation of flexible cables in a highly viscous fluid. Regions of parameter space corresponding to infinitely long, semi-infinite, and finite length curves are delineated. Almost all curves subtend an angle less than $π$ radians, but curious special cases with doubled or infinite range occur on the borders between regions. Separate transitions in the tension behavior, and counterintuitive results regarding finite towing tensions for infinitely long cables, are presented. Several physically inspired boundary value problems are solved and discussed.

items.title: The directions of science: How we search the unknown
items.summary: Science is producing knowledge at unprecedented scale, while artificial intelligence promises to accelerate the generation of hypotheses, analyses, and scientific outputs further. Yet increasing the volume of research does not necessarily expand the range of directions science effectively explores. We argue that science can be understood as a collective search process in which finite resources are allocated across an evolving space of possible research trajectories. Careers, funding, organization, publication, attention, and technology act as interacting selection mechanisms that shape this allocation. This Perspective distinguishes the visible diversity of scientific activity from its effective diversity: apparently different researchers, institutions, or projects need not provide genuinely different routes of exploration or evaluation. Our principal contribution is to introduce cross-stage dependence, which occurs when selection processes operating at different stages of science are not fully independent in the grounds through which they favour scientific trajectories. We hypothesize that, under uncertainty, repeated filtering through overlapping criteria, information, prior selections, or technological infrastructure can reduce the capacity of science to maintain plausible alternatives and redirect effort when evidence changes their relative promise. Artificial intelligence makes this problem increasingly consequential because it can simultaneously expand scientific search capacity and participate across multiple stages of production and selection. The challenge is therefore not simply to produce more knowledge, but to preserve sufficiently distinct routes of exploration, verification and correction while retaining the ability to change direction.

items.title: Nonhomogeneous elastic turbulence in the two-dimensional Taylor-Couette flow
items.summary: Elastic turbulence is a spatially and temporally disordered flow state appearing in viscoelastic fluids at vanishing fluid inertia and large elasticity. The resulting flows have broad technological interest, particularly to enhance mixing and heat transfer in microdevices. Although its experimental characterization is now well established in different setups, its theoretical understanding and numerical reproducibility remain challenging, especially in wall-bounded geometries. By means of numerical simulations, we investigate the onset of elastic turbulence and the characteristics of the developed turbulent-like states in the two-dimensional, confined, Taylor-Couette system. First, we characterize the purely elastic instability, addressing previously contrasting evidence. We then show that the fully nonlinear dynamics are weakly anisotropic and strongly nonhomogeneous. Indeed, they are confined in a dynamically active region adjacent to the inner wall, akin to the elastic boundary layer from previous predictions. Within this region, in spite of some non-negligible deviations due to the nonhomogeneity of our setup, the statistical and spectral turbulent properties are to a reasonable extent not far from the theoretical expectations and experimental observations.

items.title: Potential Flow, Stress, and Straightness in Flow Matching: Euler Error on Gaussian-Mixture Targets
items.summary: In linear flow matching, coupling straightness measures conditional displacement variance. The conditional covariance gives a kinetic stress in the Jeans balance. The virial identity relates the mean trace of the covariance to a radial moment of acceleration. Euler error also depends on how the flow propagates acceleration. On constructed Gaussian-mixture targets, closed-form couplings with matched straightness yield different median Euler errors. Learned fields from fresh minibatch assignments also yield different Euler errors from their partners at matched estimated straightness. The leading Euler coefficient accounts for more of the error variation than straightness in these experiments. We relate the additive-noise characterization of isotropic Gaussian sources to potential flow. A gradient constraint reduces velocity error on the independent isotropic Gaussian example and increases it on two examples with rotational exact fields.

items.title: Active flow control based on topological data analysis and a DMDc reduced-order model for drag reduction
items.summary: Controlling and reducing undesirable vortical structures in unsteady flows is a major issue in aerodynamics. This paper presents an active control methodology that combines topological data analysis (TDA) through persistence diagrams, a reduced-order model based on dynamic mode decomposition with control (DMDc) and receding-horizon model predictive control (MPC). Vortices are detected and characterised by the persistence diagram of the absolute value of the vorticity, which makes it possible to define a target flow in which only the useful vortices are retained. This target flow is computed offline in the reduced space by gradient descent, the derivative of a persistence diagram being defined through a parametrisation of the space of diagrams. The control loop then reduces to a small-dimensional convex quadratic program, whose construction we detail and whose cost we compare with that of an approach that places the diagrams directly in the cost function. The approach is applied numerically to the flow around an oscillating aircraft wing for seven vibration frequencies, and yields a mean reduction of the drag coefficient while preserving the main vortices.

items.title: On the wake and flapping dynamics of different aspect ratio flags
items.summary: The flapping of flags is a classical problem involving fast, large amplitude deformations of a thin flexible plate and unsteady flow phenomena. We perform systematic time- and space-resolved measurements of the deformation and drag acting on flapping flags for various aspect ratios and mass ratios. Flag deformations travel from the root to the tip while growing in amplitude. We present a robust method to determine the travelling wave properties, and reveal that the dimensionless wavelength $λ/L$ is constant for a given flutter mode, and that the wave speed equals the freestream velocity for aspect ratios above unity but decreases with decreasing mass and aspect ratio. We provide a mechanistic explanation of the influence of mass and aspect ratio on the flapping dynamics by introducing a mass-ratio-corrected dimensionless wave speed, which is proportional to the square root of the dynamic pressure difference across the flag. At smaller aspect ratio, the local dynamic pressure exerted by the fluid on the flag is reduced, leading to a decrease in the wave propagation speed and the tip frequency. Based on near wake flow field measurements, we identified two characteristic length scales, the ratio of flag area over its perimeter $L^*$ and the square root of area $\sqrt{HL}$ that scale the circulation of vortices shed per cycle. Values of the mean drag coefficient scatter widely, from \num{0} to \num{0.55}, when varying mass and aspect ratio. We can collapse the data when using a kinematics-based model with the mass ratio and the tip speed as inputs.

items.title: Radiation in relativistic plasmas via particle simulations
items.summary: We investigate radiation in relativistic electron-proton isotropic plasmas using molecular dynamics, with velocity-dependent inertia, retarded interactions, and quantum-corrected pair potentials. Radiation spectra from the Liénard-Wiechert fields agree with analytical models. Successive scattering events suppress bremsstrahlung even at weak coupling, while jitter radiation becomes comparable at higher coupling for all resolved frequencies. This first-principles framework will help develop radiation models for suppression and field effects that are inaccessible in typical particle-in-cell methods.

items.title: Bond Anharmonicity in a Caged Molecule Probed by Vibronic Core Spectroscopy
items.summary: X-ray absorption spectroscopy and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering at the nitrogen K-edge show that the N$\equiv$N bond in N$_2$@C$_{60}$ is substantially more anharmonic than in free N$_2$, with the ground-state ($X^1Σ_g^+$) anharmonic constant $\hbarω_e x_e$ a factor of two larger ($3.8\pm0.3$~meV versus $\sim 1.8$~meV) despite an essentially unchanged harmonic frequency. The same enhancement is found across all three vibronic potentials accessible to the experiment---the electronic ground state, the core-excited intermediate state, and the spectator-decay final state---pointing to a common origin rather than an effect specific to one electronic configuration. High-level coupled-cluster calculations of the N$_2$@C$_{60}$ potential energy surface, however, find no significant change in anharmonicity upon encapsulation, ruling out a simple static distortion of the N$\equiv$N bonding potential by the fullerene cage. We propose instead that the dramatic increase in $\hbarω_e x_e$ above the gas-phase value -- which, taken literally, would imply an unphysical halving of the N$_2$ dissociation energy - reflects the breakdown of the single-molecule Morse description, as previously invoked to explain anomalous anharmonicities in N$_2$ clusters, and supported by the observation of shifts in the fullerene host's Raman modes.

items.title: Evaluating a Large Language Model for Radiotherapy Patient Scheduling under Realistic Clinical and Operational Constraints: a Feasibility Study
items.summary: Radiotherapy scheduling must balance clinical constraints and operational objectives. We evaluated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate treatment schedules through simulation and retrospective clinical comparison. A one-year simulation modeled 1,400 new patients across 12 treatment categories and three linear accelerators (LINACs). Structured prompts provided ChatGPT with patient information, schedule status, clinical rules, and operational objectives. Scenarios assessed treatment-time consistency, LINAC continuity, gap reduction, and handling of infeasible requests. LLM schedules were compared with heuristic and constraint programming (CP-SAT) approaches under two objective settings. A six-week retrospective analysis included 2,043 clinical appointments. LLM-generated schedules met all predefined feasibility constraints in the evaluated scenarios, with 98.6-98.8% of fractions within preferred treatment-time windows. Prioritizing LINAC continuity reduced switching from 52.4 +/- 2.6% to 9.4 +/- 0.6%. Gap-constrained temporal relaxation reduced average daily gaps to 47.1 +/- 8.5 minutes and Friday gaps to 89.2 +/- 18.4 minutes while maintaining low overtime. The framework identified predefined violations in infeasible requests and suggested corrective actions. Heuristic and CP-SAT methods also generated feasible schedules, with performance dependent on objective weighting. In retrospective evaluation, all approaches scheduled appointments without overtime; LLM strategies reduced mean gaps by 50.8-77.1% and improved treatment-time consistency from 86.7% to 99.5-99.9%. These findings support further evaluation of structured LLM scheduling as a human-in-the-loop decision-support approach for radiotherapy.

items.title: Wave collapse proliferation as a mechanism for anomalous dissipation and spontaneous stochasticity
items.summary: Anomalous dissipation and spontaneous stochasticity are signatures of the roughness of the inviscid limit in fluid turbulence. Spontaneous stochasticity describes the selection of a probability distribution over possible solutions rather than a single deterministic trajectory. We investigate these phenomena in a nonlinear dispersive equation undergoing finite-time blowup, known as wave collapse. Collapse is arrested by two regularization mechanisms, one dissipative and one conservative. Heuristic arguments supported by numerical simulations show that an isolated collapse has a vanishing effect in the inviscid limit and cannot alone account for either phenomenon. However, simulations reveal that the number of collapse events diverges as the regularization vanishes. Their proliferation enables sustained dissipation in the dissipative case and prevents either regularization from selecting a single inviscid solution. We then introduce vanishingly small random perturbations and find numerical evidence for a well-defined statistical limit in which randomness persists. These results identify collapse proliferation as a mechanism connecting anomalous dissipation and spontaneous stochasticity in dispersive waves, allowing a formally deterministic equation to acquire a truly random limiting evolution.

items.title: A Multiscale Analysis of an Interplanetary Shock from IMAP, SOLAR-1, and the L1 Constellation to Earth
items.summary: Collisionless shocks are primary sites of particle acceleration throughout the Universe. Transient, mesoscale structures forming around these shocks influence their energy conversion efficiency, yet remain poorly observed at interplanetary (IP) shocks: spacecraft sample the shock transition briefly, and single-point measurements cannot disentangle temporal evolution from spatial structure. Here, we examine a fast, CME-driven IP shock of 2026 January 19, observed by IMAP, SOLAR-1, Wind, ACE, DSCOVR, and Aditya-L1 at L1 and by ARTEMIS and MMS near Earth, to determine its spatial and temporal structure. At MHD scales, a pre-existing solar wind flux tube is overtaken by the shock as it crosses the L1 fleet. This inflates the apparent magnetic compression ratio far beyond the ideal strong-shock limit of 4, showing that upstream and downstream intervals can sample different plasma and bias single-spacecraft estimates. At kinetic scales, IMAP and SOLAR-1, separated by only $\sim$7 $R_E$ ($\sim$340 ion inertial lengths), sample the same foreshock yet record localized structures that differ measurably; these are the first candidate signatures of large-scale foreshock transients at an IP shock. Further upstream, shocklets appear hundreds of $R_E$ ahead of the shock, consistent with steepening of ambient solar wind waves. Near Earth, the shock-to-flux-tube arrival lag increases to approximately six minutes, corresponding to a nominal sheath extension of $\sim$50 $R_E$, indicating sheath expansion over $\sim$200 $R_E$ of propagation. Together, these results show that the IP shock, its foreshock, and its sheath evolve across multiple scales from L1 to Earth, underscoring the need for multipoint measurements to resolve the underlying processes.

items.title: AI for Parameter Selection in Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization
items.summary: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) methods provide a way to compute molecular ground-state energies, but their accuracy and runtime depend sensitively on configuration choices such as the subspace dimension, propagation timestep, and the allocation of a fixed sampling budget across circuits, for which no formal selection method exists. In this work, we explore whether oracle models can predict the quantum runtime and approximation error from the Hamiltonian and the candidate configuration. Using synthetic Hamiltonians with controllable spectral properties, we show that machine-learned models can map a Hamiltonian directly to the best-ranked configuration within a predefined grid for the SKQD algorithm, validated against classical Krylov propagation, achieving strong rank correlations between true and predicted error and runtime, Spearman $ρ= 0.969$ and $ρ= 0.905$, respectively. Extending the approach to 50 molecular Hamiltonians (20-50 qubits), with reference ground-state energies from classical calculations, we train regressors that predict the simulation error and runtime for a given molecule--configuration pair ahead of execution, and classifiers to distinguish, from 600 SqDRIFT quantum-hardware runs, whether a configuration achieves a ground-state energy within chemical accuracy ($1.6\times10^{-3}$ Ha $\approx 1$ kcal/mol). For the molecular Hamiltonians, the models additionally provide an a priori feasibility and resource estimate, predicting whether a molecule can reach chemical accuracy on current hardware and at what runtime, thus correctly classifying held-out molecules at the molecule level, achieving balanced accuracy 61.8% in-distribution and 100% for five larger held-out molecules.

items.title: CGTransformer: A Topology-Aware Autoregressive Framework for Crystal Generation and Inverse Design
items.summary: Autoregressive language models offer a unified route to crystal generation and inverse design, but their performance depends on how periodic structures are serialized. Symmetry equivalent and closely related crystals can receive different atomic orders under coordinate-based serialization, introducing variability unrelated to their structural connectivity. Here, we present CGTransformer (Crystal Graph Transformer), an autoregressive generative framework that addresses this challenge via a graph-embedded sorting strategy. Using quotientgraph topology and barycentric embeddings, Element Symmetry Graph (ESG) converts periodic crystal networks into topology-guided one-dimensional sequences that retain key local and symmetry-related structural information. CGTransformer achieves high generation validity and the highest single shot crystal structure prediction (CSP) match rate among the compared MP-20 baselines (63.24%), while same backbone comparisons show improved structure recovery over coordinate-based ordering. Furthermore, we demonstrate property-conditioned inverse design for wide-bandgap semiconductors, where ESG achieves a much higher stable, unique and novel (S.U.N.) rate and stronger target-property alignment than the coordinate-based baseline. These results establish topology-guided sequence construction as an effective route to improving crystal generation and property-directed design at fixed model capacity.

items.title: Scan-specific k-space interpolation using deep Koopman autoencoders
items.summary: Purpose: To develop a scan-specific, interpretable k-space interpolation technique for the reconstruction of accelerated MRI data. Methods: A deep Koopman autoencoder for nonlinear k-space interpolation was developed consisting of an encoder, a linear layer for interpolation and a decoder. The resulting network is implemented using mean square error loss function on k-space neighbourhoods derived from the autocalibration signals (ACS), combining a prediction loss and an autoencoding loss. The approach was compared to GRAPPA and RAKI in 281 retrospectively undersampled brain datasets, using quantitative reconstruction metrics. In a subset of 52 randomly selected images, a clinical reader study compared the proposed approach and RAKI in a forced choice scenario and using a five-point ordinal scoring, assessing sharpness, SNR, aliasing and overall image quality. Additionally, the effect of varying parameters such as the number of autocalibration signals, the contribution of the autoencoding loss, the kernel size, and the latent space dimension for the proposed technique was studied. Results: The proposed approach showed improved quantitative metrics compared to GRAPPA and RAKI. Visually, the method showed higher resilience to noise amplification and improved preservation of sharp details. In the clinical reader study, the proposed approach was preferred overall to RAKI and yielded higher scores than GRAPPA and RAKI. The proposed method showed robustness to parameter variations. Conclusion: Deep Learning based k-space interpolation can be achieved using a Koopman autoencoder for k-space neighbourhoods. Keywords: Parallel imaging, Koopman autoencoder, nonlinear mapping, k-space interpolation, deep learning reconstruction

items.title: A Variational Latent Equilibrium for Learning in Neuronal Circuits
items.summary: Brains remain unrivaled in their ability to recognize and generate complex spatiotemporal patterns. While AI is able to reproduce some of these capabilities, deep learning algorithms remain largely at odds with our current understanding of brain circuitry and dynamics. This is prominently the case for backpropagation through time (BPTT), the go-to algorithm for learning complex temporal dependencies. In this work we propose a general formalism to approximate BPTT in a controlled, biologically plausible manner. Our approach builds on, unifies and extends several previous approaches to local, time-continuous, phase-free spatiotemporal credit assignment based on principles of energy conservation and extremal action. Our starting point is a prospective energy function of neuronal states, from which we calculate real-time error dynamics for time-continuous neuronal networks. With this, as a first contribution we provide a simple and straightforward derivation of the adjoint method dynamical equations, the time-continuous equivalent to BPTT. Importantly, additional approximations are necessary to avoid unphysical temporal non-localities. One such approximation was recently proposed in Generalized Latent Equilibrium (GLE), but enforcing temporal locality of the backpropagating dynamics induces an error in the gain that becomes problematic when processing complex signals. Thus, our second contribution is to design a learning rule for the backward weights to find a fully local (in space and time) set of equations for neuron and synapse dynamics that corrects for this gain difference. With this inclusion of backward weight learning, our theory provides a rigorous framework for spatiotemporal deep learning in the brain, while simultaneously advancing a blueprint for physical circuits capable of carrying out these computations.

items.title: Improved lower bound for the two-way-assisted quantum capacity of the bosonic thermal-loss channel
items.summary: The bosonic thermal-loss channel is a fundamental model for quantum communication. This Gaussian channel models the transmission of bosonic systems subject to both loss and thermal noise. It describes many practical systems, including optical fibres, waveguides and free-space links, where background thermal noise is significant. Determining the channel's two-way-assisted quantum capacity, the maximum rate at which quantum information can be transmitted reliably through the channel with two-way classical assistance, remains an open problem. Here, we improve upon the best known lower bound for this capacity for a wide range of channel parameters. We achieve this by combining an improved qubit-bosonic distribution technique with a recently introduced technique for discovering entanglement distillation protocols.

items.title: Commercial AlGaAs diodes provide simplified feedback for adaptive femtosecond pulse compression
items.summary: Maintaining high peak power in ultrashort laser pulses is essential for efficient nonlinear interactions, particularly in multiphoton microscopy. Dispersion introduced by optical components broadens these pulses and degrades their peak power, thus motivating adaptive pulse compression guided by pulse-width-dependent feedback. However, the conventional second-harmonic generation feedback requires a nonlinear crystal, spectral filtering, and careful optical alignment. Here, we investigate commercially available AlGaAs laser and light-emitting diodes as alternative two-photon absorption feedback sensors. Their photocurrent exhibits a quadratic dependence on average optical power and inverse dependence on pulse duration, which is consistent with the analytical model predicting maximum response for the shortest, single-peaked pulse. Both devices generated a measurable photocurrent at sub-milliwatt average power levels and showed a weaker polarization dependence than second-harmonic-generation-based solution. All three feedback methods achieved comparable mean compressed pulse durations of 210-228 fs. These results demonstrate effective adaptive pulse compression with a substantially simpler feedback.

items.title: Mechanical acclimation of bacterial growth and division across generations
items.summary: Bacteria frequently encounter mechanical confinement in natural and engineered environments, yet how an abrupt change in mechanical conditions reorganizes growth and division across generations remains poorly understood. Using single-cell time-lapse microscopy, we tracked Escherichia coli across generations following transfer from liquid culture to glass-attached or glass-gel-confined conditions. This mechanical confinement causes an immediate reduction in elongation rate, followed by a multi-generational mechanical acclimation process whose dynamics depend systematically on confinement strength. During this relaxation, division behavior becomes more heterogeneous and cells temporarily depart from canonical adder-like size regulation, exhibiting timer-like correlation signatures. Using a stochastic cell-cycle model that resolves the generation-dependent correlation signatures of different size-control strategies, we show that changes in elongation rate alone cannot account for the observed transition in growth-division coordination. Despite this transient reorganization, the birth-size distribution remains bounded and largely preserves its shape throughout acclimation. Notably, adder-like regulation is restored before the elongation rate fully recovers, revealing distinct relaxation timescales for growth and size-control dynamics. These results establish bacterial size control under mechanical confinement as a dynamical nonequilibrium process in which growth and division can transiently reorganize while global size homeostasis is maintained.

items.title: Radiation Hardness Assurance of Optical Coatings for the COMPASSO Iodine Reference
items.summary: The COMPASSO payload demonstrates compact iodine-based optical frequency references on the International Space Station (ISS), requiring optical windows and antireflective coatings that remain stable in the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) radiation environment. Radiation analysis was performed to quantify how trapped electrons, protons, and ions affect the fused-silica iodine cell and its coatings under mission-relevant shielding and exposure scenarios. The aim was to determine whether selected coatings meet the COMPASSO optical requirements after realistic LEO irradiation, identify degradation mechanisms linked to deposition technology and materials, and provide selection and qualification guidance for coatings in spaceborne iodine spectroscopy and precision optical-clock payloads. Nominal and worst-case electron, proton, and heavy-ion flux and fluence spectra for the ISS orbit were derived using the AE8/AP8, CREME96, ESP, and ISO15390 models. The ion component was assessed by simulation only, while irradiation tests used electrons and protons. Eight coating stacks produced by different deposition methods were exposed to proton and electron irradiation corresponding to nominal and worst-case mission loads. Pre- and post-irradiation characterization included reflectance and transmittance measurements, together with visual and microscopic inspection of coating integrity. These tests led to the selection of a four-layer Ta$_2$O$_5$/SiO$_2$ stack, which was used to produce the iodine cell optical window. Deposited and transferred particle fluences were calculated for this coating and all particle species, and the total ionizing dose (TID) in each layer was derived with GRAS. The selected coating will not be affected by corpuscular radiation for years in the ISS LEO environment, and the TID expected at the ISS Bartolomeo platform will not affect its optical properties.

items.title: A unified finite-site framework for scaffold-client biocondensation
items.summary: Client recruitment into biomolecular condensates does not determine how stronger binding changes the bulk free-energy advantage of demixing. Here, we use a unified finite-site thermodynamic framework to examine how scaffold-client interactions affect both the response of a fixed-composition mixture and the organization of its ternary phase diagram. The thermodynamic response to increasing client affinity is determined by the difference in heterotypic bonding between the complete equilibrium phase-separated sample and the corresponding homogeneous state. A finite region of the model exhibits positive scaffold-client concentration covariance but negative heterotypic bond contrast: stronger binding reduces the demixing advantage even when both species enrich in the dense phase. This reduction also occurs with independent scaffold self-association and client-binding site pools, without direct displacement of scaffold bonds. A negative response does not by itself imply condensate shrinkage or dissolution. Across composition space, the same finite binding constraints support scaffold-rich and heterotypic coexistence regimes with distinct bond populations. For divalent clients, these regimes can occupy disconnected regions of the phase diagram and reconnect upon increasing client affinity, depending on scaffold cohesion. Critical-point continuation identifies the folds and cusp organizing these changes, while client valence restricts the parameter range over which disconnected coexistence occurs. Explicit-particle Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the qualitative reentrant response and provide finite-size evidence for disconnected coexistence. These results provide a bond-resolved characterization of fixed-parent affinity response and a complementary description of coexistence under specified association constraints.

items.title: Reconciling global and local spin models
items.summary: Magnetic interactions based on first-principles calculations can be casted either into global spin models, where the interactions are configuration-independent, or into local spin models, where the effective parameters depend explicitly on the underlying spin configuration. Although these two perspectives often yield seemingly inconsistent results, we demonstrate that they can be reconciled by restricting the analysis to transverse spin fluctuations. We develop a projection scheme that systematically removes spurious longitudinal contributions from local interaction matrices, thereby establishing a rigorous connection between the projected local interactions and the underlying global multispin Hamiltonian. Applying our approach to the prototype systems (i) a Cr trimer on Au(111) (ii) Fe and Cr dimers on Cu(001), we show that the projected local interaction parameters quantitatively reproduce those obtained from the global four-spin model. This work provides a unified framework to interpret local and global spin models on equal footing and resolves long-standing ambiguities in the identification of effective interactions such as the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) in a non-collinear framework.

items.title: The Benjamin-Feir stability diagram for Stokes waves with constant vorticity in finite depth
items.summary: We determine the Benjamin-Feir stability diagram for small-amplitude Stokes waves with constant vorticity in finite depth. For the full water wave system, we derive an explicit instability index and rigorously classify its sign throughout the depth-vorticity plane. With gravitational acceleration and carrier wavenumber normalized to one, we identify a unique minimum depth $h_{\text{crit}}\approx1.36271$, below which Benjamin-Feir instability is absent for every vorticity. Above this depth, two vorticity thresholds delimit the unstable regime, outside of which the spectrum near the origin remains purely imaginary for all small Floquet exponents. In particular, at each fixed finite depth, constant vorticity of sufficiently large magnitude suppresses Benjamin-Feir instability. Moreover, any constant vorticity $γ\ge 2/\sqrt{3}$ suppresses Benjamin-Feir instability at every finite depth. The proof combines Hamiltonian spectral perturbation theory, symbolic computations, and formal verification in Rocq. Away from the transition set, our results rigorously confirm the stability criterion predicted by the nonlinear Schrödinger approximation of Thomas, Kharif, and Manna.

items.title: Symmetry-breaking and hysteretic transitions in an actively coupled optical trimer
items.summary: We investigate the nonlinear dynamics of a non-Hermitian optical trimer consisting of three lossy waveguides with complex-valued coupling. Building on our previous analysis of its global dynamics, we adopt a site-resolved approach to elucidate the bifurcation structure and the organization of oscillatory states across the individual waveguides. We identify a hysteretic transition from reflection-asymmetric periodic states to periodic states exhibiting a combined reflection-translation symmetry. This transition involves a double-loop hysteretic regime characterized by the coexistence of multiple attractors. Analysis of the spatial intensity profiles and their Fourier spectra reveals distinct oscillatory behavior among the waveguides.
