We addressed this with the Watanabe Illusion, a stimulus not previously studied quantitatively: an oblique segment inside a circle whose extension geometrically hits the topmost of 11 dots, yet human observers (n = 131) reported a dot near the middle of the column. Five VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 7B, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.5 Instant, Gemini 3.5 Flash), given the identical stimulus and wording, all deviated in the same direction. In the open-weight Qwen2.5-VL-32B, linear probes on the vision encoder recovered the line angle and the target dot six to eight times more accurately than its behavioral responses. A layer-wise logit lens showed that the correct answer dominates in the middle layers of the language model and is overwritten in late layers only under a visual-judgment frame. Naming the illusion, requesting suppression of prior knowledge, forcing a visual chain of thought, and 390 semantic preambles left the response center unchanged; only disclosing the correct answer moved it. VLMs may therefore carry human perceptual biases at the language-generation stage, where they resist declarative correction.

items.title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Lossy Transmission and Rogers' Paradox
items.summary: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, such as fresh human data, verifiers, or curators, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given. We argue that cultural evolution has a theory of the supply, and that it distinguishes two ways copying loses knowledge. In a fixed world, copies are lossy, as in Henrich's account of skill loss in small populations. In a changing world, even perfect copies go stale, which is Rogers' paradox. We write both as one chain with separately measurable parameters and test it on lineages of language models (word trigrams and a character transformer on two books, and OPT-125m on wikitext-2, on arXiv abstracts written after its pretraining, and on a world of 2,000 fictional facts that change at a set rate). In a fixed world, neutral drift on word frequencies predicts, with no free parameter, the rare-word coverage of every trigram lineage to within 0.03. In the fact world, the model's accuracy falls and its outdated answers rise with the rate of change; the chain calibrated on the static world predicts both for mid- and low-frequency facts to within 0.03 on average, with the rate of change set, not fitted. Models that inherit their weights keep more in a static world and carry more outdated facts in a changing one, as Rogers' theory says of individual memory. Finally we close the loop with the people who write the data. When they can ask the model instead of finding out, the model ends up exactly as reliable as finding out is costly, and in both regimes someone must keep paying to learn; we give the share in closed form, extend it to lossy copying, heterogeneous costs, aggregating models, and users who check, and show when checking is a stable way out.

items.title: S1Pert: Scalable Target-Specific Gene Response Prediction with System-One Intelligence
items.summary: Predicting transcriptional responses to unseen genetic perturbations is essential for extending CRISPR screens across vast target--gene combinations. However, models can achieve strong aggregate predictive performance by reproducing historical gene-level response frequencies without adequately distinguishing the effects of different perturbations. Reliable prediction at the transcriptome scale is further challenged by uncertain response labels and redundant computation across millions of target--gene pairs. We present S1Pert, a System-One framework for target-specific gene response prediction with non-autoregressive online inference. S1Pert combines directional Welch tests and equivalence testing to distinguish statistically supported responses from inconclusive observations. A frozen System-One encoder extracts reusable semantic representations of perturbation targets, query genes, and historical evidence. Compact pair-specific interactions are then computed and cached offline. A lightweight hierarchical cross-attention decoder integrates these representations with cross-target pairwise ranking and synchronized historical-evidence dropout to reduce reliance on gene-level response frequencies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that S1Pert improves target-specific response discrimination while maintaining reliable prediction and efficient inference across diverse cellular contexts. These findings highlight the potential of System-One decision learning for scalable perturbation-response prediction beyond historical gene-level response tendencies. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/liujiawen-jpg/S1Pert.

items.title: A Minimal Quantitative Model of Perceptual Suppression and Breakthrough in Visual Rivalry
items.summary: When conflicting images are presented to either eye, binocular fusion is disrupted. Rather than experiencing a blend of both percepts, often only one eye's image is experienced, whilst the other is suppressed from awareness. Importantly, suppression is transient - the two rival images compete for dominance, with stochastic switches between mutually exclusive percepts occurring every few seconds with law-like regularity. From the perspective of dynamical systems theory, visual rivalry offers an experimentally tractable window into the dynamical mechanisms governing perceptual awareness. In a recently developed visual rivalry paradigm - tracking continuous flash suppression (tCFS) - it was shown that the transition between awareness and suppression is hysteretic, with a higher contrast threshold required for a stimulus to breakthrough suppression into awareness than to be suppressed from awareness. Here, we present an analytically-tractable model of visual rivalry that quantitatively explains the hysteretic transition between periods of awareness and suppression in tCFS. Grounded in the theory of neural dynamics, we derive closed-form expressions for the duration of perceptual dominance and suppression, and for the degree of hysteresis (i.e. the depth of perceptual suppression), as a function of model parameters. Finally, our model yields a series of novel behavioural predictions, the first of which - distributions of dominance and suppression durations during tCFS should be approximately equal - we empirically validate in human psychophysical data.

items.title: High-Fidelity 3D Simulator for Synthetic fNIRS Data Generation
items.summary: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides a noninvasive window into brain activity by measuring task-related changes in oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin in the cortex. However, analyzing fNIRS data is challenging because of motion artifacts, physiological noise, and other confounding factors. This challenge is further compounded by the limited availability of annotated datasets, which hinders the development and validation of new analysis pipelines, particularly given the growing use of AI methods. Recognizing these challenges, we introduce a 3D fNIRS simulator that uses mesh-based Monte Carlo simulations to generate physiologically informed, full-head synthetic recordings with controllable spatiotemporal characteristics. Our simulator combines anatomically informed sensitivity profiles with parameterized models of hemodynamic responses, systemic physiology, and measurement artifacts. As a result, users can generate large labeled datasets with known cortical ground truth for developing and evaluating denoising algorithms, data augmentation strategies, mechanistic models, and in silico experiments. We validate key spatiotemporal and physiological properties of the simulator against experimental fNIRS data from open-source finger-tapping, pain-assessment, and surgical-skill datasets.

items.title: Directional Confusions Reveal Divergent Inductive Biases Through Rate-Distortion Geometry in Human and Machine Vision
items.summary: Humans and modern vision models can reach similar classification accuracy while making systematically different kinds of mistakes -- differing not in how often they err, but in who gets mistaken for whom and in which direction. We show that these directional confusions reveal distinct inductive biases that are invisible to accuracy alone. Using matched human and deep vision model responses on a natural-image categorization task under 12 perturbation types, we quantify asymmetry in confusion matrices and link it to the shape of the information-error trade-off. We characterize this trade-off geometry using three signatures extracted from the rate-distortion (RD) frontier: slope beta, curvature kappa and efficiency (AUC). We find that humans exhibit broad but weak asymmetries, whereas deep vision models show sparser, stronger directional collapses. Robustness training reduces global asymmetry but fails to recover the human-like breadth-strength profile of graded similarity. Mechanistic simulations further show that different asymmetry organizations shift the RD frontier in opposite directions, even when matched for performance. Together, these results position directional confusions and RD geometry as compact, interpretable signatures of inductive bias under distribution shift.

items.title: Neural Simulation-Based Inference for Computational Cognitive Models: A Tutorial
items.summary: Computational cognitive modeling is an increasingly essential methodology to elucidate the mechanisms underlying human and animal cognition. By fitting models to empirical data, researchers can perform parameter estimation, model comparison, and model-based neural analyses to assess competing theories, quantify individual differences, and investigate neural representations. Typically, fitting these models relies on likelihood-dependent methods (e.g., Maximum likelihood estimation or hierarchical Bayesian methods). However, for many reasonable cognitive models, computing the likelihood is computationally intractable, in which case these methods become inadequate. This substantially limits the range of theories that researchers can investigate. Simulation-based inference with neural networks (neural SBI) has emerged as a powerful toolkit to overcome this hurdle. By training deep neural networks on datasets generated through model simulations, neural SBI learns the relation between observable data and cognitive models. This approach enables all the applications of standard modeling while bypassing the likelihood computation, without constraints on empirical data size. Despite its successful adoption across diverse scientific fields, neural SBI remains underutilized in cognitive modeling, partly due to a lack of accessible, domain-tailored guidance. This tutorial addresses this gap by providing a clear workflow for applying neural SBI to cognitive models. We also provide practical use cases and recommendations for reducing the computational and simulation burden, facilitating efficient implementation in real-world research settings. By lowering the technical barriers to neural SBI, this tutorial aims to empower cognitive scientists to investigate richer theory spaces and ultimately propel scientific discovery.

items.title: Attributing Cohen's d: Training Data Attribution for Disease-Related Effects in Normative Age Biomarkers
items.summary: Normative age models are trained to predict chronological age in a nominally healthy cohort. In patients, the gap between predicted and chronological age is read as disease risk. We attribute the disease-related effect size of the age gap directly to individual training samples, rather than using a prediction-level loss as the attribution target. For the Cohen's d effect size, the resulting closed-form influence functional, validated against leave-one-out retraining, ranks training samples by their effect on held-out case-control separation. Across four diseases and two biomarker modalities in UK Biobank, removing the 10% most influential training samples raises held-out disease-related effect size in every seed. It more than doubles the metabolomic-age effect for type 2 diabetes and raises the brain-age effect for multiple sclerosis by roughly a third. Random removal leaves effect size flat even at 50% removal, confirming the gain comes from which samples are removed, not how many. Flagged subjects, missed by diagnosis-based exclusion, show elevated cardiometabolic markers the model never sees, consistent with subclinical contamination of the reference cohort. For type 2 diabetes, where the method gains most, the marker recovered is HbA1c, the standard measure of blood sugar control. We release our influence-function package pyinfluence.

items.title: Domain-repetition patterns in protein domain trigrams are uniform across chromosomes and conserved among multicellular eukaryotes
items.summary: Proteins are built from domains, and the order of domains along a protein can be read like a sentence. We take every run of three consecutive Pfam domains (a domain trigram) and classify it by its pattern of repetition: all three the same (AAA), the first two (AAB), the last two (ABB), the outer two (ABA) or all different (ABC). We ask whether the proportions of these five patterns are conserved across the chromosomes of a genome and across genomes. We built a reproducible workflow and applied it to the UniProt reference proteomes of 16 organisms, from Escherichia coli to human, with Pfam 39.0. In Drosophila melanogaster, 3,107 distinct trigrams split into 63% ABC, 13% each of AAB and ABB, and 5% each of AAA and ABA. Every chromosome arm closely matches this pie: each lies within the range expected for a random set of genes of the same size. The human pie has less ABC (55%) and more AAB and ABB (18% each), and 23 of its 25 chromosomes and other components fall within the random-gene range. Pies of trigram occurrences vary more, mostly because of a few giant repeat proteins. Across 199 chromosomes and other proteome components of 14 organisms, tested with a gene-level permutation, 4 (2%) differ from their own proteome in distinct trigrams and 10 (5%) in occurrences, chiefly human and macaque chromosome 19, whose KRAB zinc-finger clusters make it rich in AAA repeats. Across organisms, the distinct-trigram pie is closely conserved among multicellular eukaryotes (ABC 55-67%, with AAB and ABB always within 2 percentage points of each other) and shifts towards ABC in yeasts (75-77%) and bacteria (82-86%). The proportion of domain-repetition patterns is therefore conserved across the chromosomes of a genome and shared by plants and animals, while repeat-rich giant proteins and tandem gene clusters account for most of the local deviations.

items.title: Mechanism-Level Chemical Reaction Simulation with Electron Bookkeeping Transformer
items.summary: Modeling chemical reaction mechanisms is central to understanding and predicting chemical reactivity. We present Electron Bookkeeping Transformer (Bookkeeper), a data-driven model that simulates chemical reactions at mechanistic resolution by generating electron movement trajectories. Following the symbolic arrow-pushing formalism in chemistry, Bookkeeper explicitly models each electron as a token and predicts its movement sequentially, ensuring mass and charge conservation during both elementary step and reaction pathway predictions by construction. On reaction-size-balanced test sets, Bookkeeper improves top-1 elementary-step accuracy, top-1 pathway rank accuracy, and top-1 to top-5 product prediction accuracy over FlowER. On the entire test set, it achieves higher elementary-step top-1 accuracy but lower pathway accuracy than FlowER. Bookkeeper also samples elementary steps substantially faster, adapts to several unseen reaction types with minimal fine-tuning, and generates candidate chemical transformations for further screening. These results suggest that explicit electron bookkeeping is a useful framework for virtually screening chemical reactions across diverse reagents, validating computer-assisted synthesis planning predictions, and providing mechanistic interpretations of reactivity.

items.title: On the Promises and Limits of Multi-omics Integration for Deconvolution: The HADACA3 Benchmark
items.summary: Understanding the cellular composition of complex tissues, such as tumors, is a key challenge in biology and medicine. A common approach, known as deconvolution, aims to estimate Understanding the cellular composition of complex tissues, such as tumours, is a key challenge in biology and medicine. Deconvolution methods estimate cell-type proportions from bulk molecular measurements, and the increasing availability of multiple molecular modalities has raised the expectation that their integration should improve estimation accuracy. However, whether and under which conditions multi-omics integration actually improves deconvolution remains unclear. Here we present HADACA3, a community-driven competition followed by a modular benchmark of more than 18,000 pipelines combining pre-processing, feature selection, deconvolution and integration of RNA and DNA methylation (DNAm), across nine pancreatic cancer datasets. With the available references, DNAm alone achieves the highest median performance, outperforming RNA alone and most integration strategies. Dataset-specific optimisation of generic integration pipelines rarely improves upon DNAm alone: the best configurations mostly reduce the weight of RNA, and their gains do not generalise across datasets. The only consistent improvement, confirmed on unseen data, comes from an integration rule that estimates cancer cell types from DNAm alone and averages both modalities for non-cancer cell types. These findings challenge the assumption that integrating more molecular data necessarily improves deconvolution. Instead, effective multi-omics integration relies on prior knowledge of the cell-type-specific strengths of each modality, rather than on generic statistical integration strategies.

items.title: Similar Predictive Fit but Different Latent Dynamics: Characterizing Learned Dynamical Structure in Personalized Models of Brain Disorders
items.summary: As AI models move toward clinical decision-making and personalized treatment, understanding \emph{what} a model learns is important beyond predictive accuracy alone. We investigate whether personalized latent dynamics reveal clinically associated differences even when predictive fit is similar. A lightweight CNN--Transformer EEG foundation model pretrained on the Temple University EEG Corpus (TUEG) extracts segment-level representations. Using the Temple University Epilepsy Corpus (TUEP), representations are mapped to a shared latent-state space, and sparse multinomial logistic transition distributions (mLTD) are fit independently to each subject to obtain personalized transition-dependency graphs $W_n$. Analyses include $n{=}198$ subjects (99 epilepsy / 99 non-epilepsy). At $k{=}4$, epilepsy subjects exhibit substantially denser learned dependency structure ($p{=}1.1\times10^{-7}$), with the same pattern at $k{=}6$ (19.90 vs. 13.46; $p{=}5.2\times10^{-5}$). Graph-derived features provide moderate group discrimination under 5-fold subject-wise cross-validation (AUROC 0.68 at $k{=}4$; 0.65 at $k{=}6$). In contrast, held-out log-likelihood is nearly identical between groups at $k{=}4$ ($-0.992$ vs. $-0.991$; $p{=}0.95$), with similarly matched next-state prediction (AUROC 0.855 vs. 0.861; $p{=}0.54$). Thus, similar predictive fit does not imply similar learned dynamics: groups can be comparably predictable while differing substantially in the internal dynamical structure learned by personalized models. This distinction motivates evaluating learned structure alongside predictive performance in personalized clinical models.

items.title: Trainable sparse dendritic networks reveal regime-dependent roles for shunting inhibition and morphology
items.summary: Neural circuits must compute with noisy inputs and adapt their responses to context. How dendritic structure and synaptic integration support these functions remains unclear. We introduce DendriNet, a trainable rate-based framework with sparse excitatory and inhibitory contacts, controllable dendritic architecture and alternative integration rules. In image-classification tasks, shunting networks transmit and rely on distal dendritic signals more strongly than additive networks. Distributing limited contacts across compartments improves classification in small populations, whereas greater serial dendritic depth provides no benefit on clean images within resource-matched trees. Robustness depends on input statistics: deeper shunting trees better tolerate independent pixel noise, while addition better tolerates strong global scaling. In a contextual task with gain variation and noise, shunting improves accuracy under the training corruption but depends less on context-specific inhibition than a separately tuned additive network. Learning leak conductances partly restores shunting accuracy on dim, noise-free inputs outside the training distribution. At AlexNet width, shunting integration and learned sparse connectivity support smaller deployed networks with accuracy comparable to retrained dense layers. These results distinguish the local action of synaptic integration from the computational roles acquired by inhibitory pathways through learning, and suggest experiments on dendritic function and design principles for brain-inspired networks.

items.title: Structure-Preserving Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Dynamics on Arbitrary Time Scales
items.summary: The leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron combines a passive membrane law with threshold-triggered firing and reset. We formulate this hybrid neuron model, under constant input, on an arbitrary Hilger time scale $\mathbb{T}$. Our central result is that, after the first spike, the firing times satisfy $t_{n+1}=Π_{\mathbb{T}}^{+}(t_n+T_c)$, where $T_c$ is the classical reset-to-threshold travel time. This recursion requires no periodicity, homogeneity, or translation invariance of $\mathbb{T}$; it holds for every time scale that is unbounded above. To preserve the passive membrane physics, we use the inverse cylinder transformation to construct a positively regressive coefficient $p_m$. The resulting delta-dynamic equation is exactly the restriction to $\mathbb{T}$ of the classical continuous-time LIF trajectory. By contrast, the direct transcription $V^Δ=-(V-V_\infty)/τ_m$ exhibits graininess-dependent sign reversal and amplification at coarse right-scattered points. The first firing time is the forward projection of the classical continuous threshold-crossing time onto $\mathbb{T}$, and, when the graininess is bounded by $μ^\ast$, the per-event forward-projection delay -- from each reset to the next realized firing time, relative to the continuous crossing time computed from that same reset -- is bounded above by $μ^\ast$. On $\mathbb{T}=h\mathbb{Z}$ we obtain the explicit lattice-quantized law $T_{\mathrm{ISI}}^{(h)}=h\lceil T_c/h\rceil$, which converges to the classical continuous-time inter-spike interval as $h\to0^+$. The framework therefore separates preserved membrane physics from the temporal opportunity structure imposed by the time domain. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic Hilger-calculus treatment of a threshold-and-reset LIF spiking neuron on an arbitrary time scale.

items.title: Using an energy pixels approach to estimate the size a 2nd Generation DEL must be to train a high-resolution binding model
items.summary: DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) are commonly used to find small-molecule binders to a target protein. But the hard part is no longer finding a hit. It is building a machine-learning model good enough to guide the medicinal chemistry that follows, one that can resolve the shift in affinity when a chemist changes a single atom. Such a model needs two things from its training data: dense sampling of the small patch of chemical space around the hit, and an adequate number of genuinely tight binders within it. A diverse naive DEL gives neither. It samples an enormous space, so any one neighborhood is covered far too thinly, and the tightest binders are rare. A model trained on that naive DEL data must extrapolate to binders tighter than any it has seen, and that is where models can fail. One way to get training data with both properties is a second-generation DEL built around the hit. We ask how complex that library must be. We treat binding as a sum of small, independent interactions, called pixels on the target and antipixels on the ligand. From the spread of affinities measured in the naive library, with no structural information and nothing yet synthesized, we estimate the complexity such a library must have to supply that dense sampling and those tight binders. The method does two useful things. It turns the number of tight binders a model needs into the number of compounds a library must contain. And it estimates the expected yield of a randomly designed second-generation DEL, so the gain from designing the library with machine learning or active learning can be measured against a baseline, without the expense of a control library as large as the experiment itself.

items.title: Reduced rank regression for neural communication: a tutorial for neuroscientists
items.summary: Reduced rank regression (RRR) is a statistical method for finding a low-dimensional linear mapping between a set of high-dimensional inputs and outputs. In recent years, RRR has found numerous applications in neuroscience, in particular for identifying "communication subspaces" governing the interactions between brain regions. This tutorial article seeks to provide an introduction to RRR and its mathematical foundations, with a particular emphasis on neural communication. We discuss RRR's relationship to alternate dimensionality reduction techniques such as singular value decomposition (SVD), principal components analysis (PCA), principal components regression (PCR), and canonical correlation analysis (CCA). We also derive important extensions to RRR, including ridge regularization and non-spherical noise. Finally, we introduce new metrics for quantifying communication strength as well as the alignment between communication axes and the principal modes of neural activity. By the end of this article, readers should have a clear understanding of RRR and the practical considerations involved in applying it to their own data.

items.title: Species differences dilute the stabilizing effect of higher-order interactions in competitive communities
items.summary: Higher-order interactions, in which the presence of a third species modulates the interaction between two others, have been proposed as a mechanism that stabilizes ecological communities. In particular, in models of intransitive competition, replacing pairwise contests by three-way contests turns neutral oscillations into a stable coexistence equilibrium. Whether this stabilizing effect survives in more realistic scenarios, when pairwise and higher-order interactions act together, species differ in their demographic rates, and interactions take place on a network remains unclear. Here, we study a competitive community model with a tunable fraction $α$ of higher-order interactions, combining Lyapunov and linear stability analysis with numerical simulations and empirical birth and mortality rates of plants. For identical species, any $α>0$ makes the coexistence equilibrium globally stable. Differences among species in the ratio of birth to mortality rates, instead, make pairwise competition actively destabilizing and shift the transition to a finite critical fraction $α_c$, which grows with the variance of these ratios. For larger differences, a feasible equilibrium often ceases to exist and, when it exists, higher-order interactions frequently fail to stabilize it. Even when stable, the coexistence equilibrium is often only one of two attractors near the transition, so that robust coexistence requires a larger fraction of higher-order interactions. On sparse random hypergraphs, a finite fraction is needed even for identical species: coexistence requires each individual to take part, on average, in more than one higher-order interaction, well beyond the percolation of hyperlinks. Our results show that the claimed stabilizing effect of higher-order interactions is fragile, and depends jointly on species differences and on the structure of interactions.

items.title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. Biological foundation models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein, and single-cell measurements predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Agentic systems, AI assistants built on large language models, can run multistep analyses from plain-language requests and increasingly call foundation models as tools. Yet it is often unclear when these models' outputs can be trusted. We frame this as a model's knowledge boundary: the range of inputs, tasks, and conditions over which its outputs are reliable. This review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis) define this boundary. We examine evidence on where current models succeed or fail and present standardized descriptions of model limits so that researchers, and the agents acting for them, can use these tools reliably.

items.title: Random Exploration is Random
items.summary: Decision making often requires balancing exploitation of familiar options with exploration of uncertain alternatives. One strategy for exploration is random exploration, in which choices become more variable and less tied to the option that currently appears best. However, it remains unclear whether this variability reflects genuine stochasticity or instead a deterministic structure that traditional cognitive models fail to capture. We examined this question using the Horizon Task in an aggregated dataset of 1,392 participants completing over 1,270,695 trials. In this task, exploration becomes more valuable when participants have more future choices, and choice variability increases under longer horizons. We tested whether more expressive neural network models could recover deterministic structure from this additional variability. Although neural networks provided better overall fits to behavior than the traditional model, long-horizon choices remained consistently less predictable than short-horizon choices. These findings show that limited model expressiveness cannot fully account for the increased variability associated with random exploration, suggesting random exploration truly is substantially random.

items.title: Dynamical mean-field theory of latching Potts networks
items.summary: Spontaneous transitions between memories, as observed in internally generated cognition such as mind-wandering and free association, require neural dynamics capable of destabilizing one attractive memory state and moving towards another. We ask what minimal representational structure is required for such transitions to emerge in random associative networks. To address this question, we study Potts associative networks with $S$ active states per unit and slow adaptive thresholds. The $S=1$ case can model a standard Hopfield-like network of binary units. We employ dynamical mean-field theory in the extensive-load regime, where the number of stored patterns scales linearly with network size and connectivity, and we focus on transitions between two condensed memories, which are singled out in the connectivity matrix. In the finite-load regime, we show that transitions are governed by an effective drive term, whose sign and temporal evolution distinguish high-latching (structured), low-latching (random), and non-latching regimes. The resulting phase diagram shows that adaptation alone is not sufficient: transitions only occur within certain ranges of the overlap between the two memories. In the binary case $S=1$, in particular, no unit can be active in both memories but in different Potts states, thus strongly supressing the high-latching, structured transitions that exist for $S>1$. In the extensive-load regime, non-condensed memories generate colored fluctuations and retarded self-interactions through an effective memory kernel. We find that latching trajectories change the effective timescale of this kernel, a dynamical signature of transitions in the extensive-load regime. These results indicate that multi-state Potts-like representations are essential for structured memory-to-memory transitions, a hallmark of spontaneous thought.

items.title: Universal Infectious Disease Forecasting with Mantis 2
items.summary: Public health agencies need to anticipate how outbreaks will unfold, when they will peak, and how long demand on health services will remain elevated. We previously developed a foundation model, Mantis, which was trained entirely on simulated outbreaks---enabling us to generate the diversity and scale of training data needed to support forecasting across diseases. However, our previous work left unresolved when simulation improves predictions and how it should complement observational data. Here, we varied the balance of simulated and observed training data while holding forecasting tasks fixed and varying the available surveillance history. We found that simulation-rich training was particularly valuable with limited local history, and its relative advantage diminished as more observations became available. We also found that simulation-based training reduced exceptionally large forecast errors, suggesting that mechanistic knowledge can help compensate for limited local evidence. Building on these findings, we developed Mantis 2, which combines simulated and observational training to jointly forecast up to six variables sixteen weeks ahead. Across 30 forecasting tasks, Mantis 2 achieved the best aggregate probabilistic accuracy over short, medium, and long horizons among the machine learning, statistical, and baseline models evaluated. It missed roughly 30\% fewer outbreak peaks than the strongest comparison model, with successfully anticipated peaks identified more than six weeks in advance on average. We publicly release Mantis 2, enabling public health agencies and researchers to forecast disease outcomes without developing a separate model for each disease or location.

items.title: On the minimum energy required to trigger a spike
items.summary: We formulate and numerically study the problem of finding the minimum energy required to trigger a spike in a three-dimensional conductance-based excitable model. The variational formulation seeks a state trajectory that reaches the boundary of the spiking region with the least \textit{peak} cumulative work supplied through the membrane port. We approximate voltage histories by sums of real exponentials, reducing the problem to a finite-dimensional optimization. The best-found voltage waveform consists of a hyperpolarization phase followed by a depolarization phase, which seems to match the experimentally determined optimal stimulus in squid giant axons.

items.title: Diversification under Global Competition: A Cutoff-Induced Localization Mechanism
items.summary: Niche differentiation promotes biological diversity but does not necessarily eliminate competition for shared limiting resources. What determines the extent of diversity when evolutionary diversification takes place under such constraints? We investigate this question using a simple, analytically tractable model combining mutations in continuous trait space, local competition, and global competition for shared resources. We show that, without an establishment threshold, the population spreads indefinitely in trait space even as its total abundance approaches a finite limit. In contrast, an arbitrarily small establishment threshold allows a stable localized distribution. Together with mortality induced by global competition, the threshold creates bistability, and global feedback drives the system exponentially close to the Maxwell point, where an isolated invasion front is stationary. The resulting soliton has height $H\propto\varepsilon^{2/3}$ and width $W\propto\varepsilon^{-2/3}$. Simulations with discrete individuals reveal an archipelago of fluctuating clusters whose spatial extent eventually reaches statistical saturation, unlike the continuous deterministic soliton. Nevertheless, an effective cutoff $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}\simeq0.8/(N\sqrtμ)$ reproduces the observed scaling of the population mass deficit. Remarkably, both occupied trait-site richness and effective species richness exhibit approximately the same scaling as the deterministic soliton width. Thus, deterministic cutoff theory captures global diversity scaling despite failing to reproduce the community's spatial organization.

items.title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
items.summary: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.

items.title: A risk-aware individualized blood pressure target to avoid hypotension in surgery
items.summary: We propose an online method for choosing both a blood pressure target and a norepinephrine dose for an individual surgical patient. From a short record of mean arterial pressure (MAP) and norepinephrine delivery, the method fits a reduced pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic model and uses a local Gaussian approximation to propagate uncertainty to future MAP readings. It searches for the lowest target for which a bolus and constant infusion keep the predicted probability of at least one MAP reading below 65 mmHg after the rise phase within a prescribed limit. If no such target is found, the decision returns to the clinician. We assess calibration of the predicted minimum MAP on retrospective surgical records under the doses actually administered. In a cohort of 4,096 virtual patients, the method recommended a dose for 74 % of patients at a nominal risk of 5 %. Among the patients receiving a recommendation, 6.9 % had a reading below 65 mmHg. A fixed target of 70 mmHg yielded a rate of 25 % when applied to the full virtual cohort.

items.title: Similarity-Guided Optimization Strategies for Approximate Network Symmetry Detection
items.summary: Symmetry in complex networks is a structural property with broad implications for network function, dynamics, and robustness. While classical approaches rely on exact automorphisms and thus remain highly sensitive to small perturbations, recent work of Liu has introduced approximate formulations that relax the strict invariance condition and recast symmetry detection as an optimization problem over permutations. We investigate how node-level similarity information can be used to bias the search toward structurally plausible vertex correspondences, with network centralities serving as one interpretable instance. Building on this perspective, we adapt simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, tabu search, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution and the quadratic symmetry approximator to this problem, add similarity guidance to each, and introduce Bilinear Approximate Symmetry Inference (BASIN), which learns a soft assignment matrix via bilinear embeddings. Using a unified evaluation pipeline, we compare their guided and unguided variants, BASIN and a random baseline on four synthetic graph families, structural brain connectomes, and three empirical networks with known automorphism groups. Node-similarity guidance is decisive where a planted orbit exists that the unguided search misses, and algorithm-dependent elsewhere, on synthetic and empirical networks alike. Overall, tabu search achieves the strongest performance; its guided variant (SGTS) has the lowest median score among the guided variants in all 44 synthetic conditions, while BASIN is the better of the continuous relaxations on rewired lateral graphs. The effect of node-similarity guidance is therefore regime-dependent rather than uniformly positive.

items.title: Exact power spectra and effective dimensionality in critical block-GOE networks
items.summary: Criticality in neural networks is crucial for optimal information processing. Recent studies have shifted focus from static criticality to frequency-dependent behavior, particularly in oscillatory systems modeled by block-Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (block-GOE) matrices. However, analytical tools to predict spectral properties such as power spectrum and effective dimensionality remain scarce. In this work, we derive exact solutions for the network-averaged power spectrum $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{S}(ω)]$, the network autocovariance $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{C}(τ)]$, and the normalized effective dimensionality $D_N(ω)$ in block-GOE ensembles. These results provide a comprehensive framework for understanding how oscillatory networks operate near criticality, offering insights into the dynamic balance between stability and flexibility in large-scale neural systems.

items.title: MutAtlas: A PDB-Wide Energy-Guided Atlas of Protein Mutation Effects
items.summary: Protein mutation effect prediction is fundamental to protein engineering and disease variant interpretation, yet experimentally measured mutation data remain accurate but extremely sparse. To provide scalable supplementary mutation signals, we construct a PDB-wide mutation augmentation dataset that exhaustively enumerates single-site substitutions on experimentally resolved protein structures and aligns mutation signals from physics-based energy models, protein language models, and inverse folding models. Large-scale analysis under a unified mutation preference representation reveals substantial differences in the consistency, concentration, and substitution patterns of mutation distributions across models, indicating that disagreement is pervasive and reflects conflicting inductive biases rather than random noise. Motivated by these observations, we propose an unsupervised multi-source mutation preference distillation framework that learns from relative mutation preferences while explicitly modeling cross-source disagreement. Without using any experimental mutation labels during training, our approach achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated zero-shot baselines and naive multi-source fusion strategies on ProteinGym. We release the dataset and evaluation pipeline to support reproducible studies of protein mutation effects.

items.title: Confident and Wrong: Structure Confidence Is a Poor Selection Filter for Protein Function
items.summary: Structure-guided protein design can generate plausible candidates, but structural confidence does not predict function. We trained a function-guided model on measured metal-binding affinity with protein sequence, ligand identity, and assay conditions, and used it to design rare earth element (REE) binding variants of lanmodulin, a lanthanide-binding protein with four EF-hand domains. We screened 297 designs from three strategies against terbium and dysprosium, adjacent lanthanides among the hardest REE pairs to separate. Selection on structural confidence inverted the outcome it was meant to improve. The Structure-Confidence-Selected panel carried the highest pTM, complex ipLDDT, and composite confidence scores, and expressed at 97%, yet only 16.7% of its designs bound terbium (95% CI 10.4 to 25.7), against 83.3% (74.6 to 89.5) for the function-guided panel, whose confidence scores were the lowest. The odds of binding differed 25-fold between the two panels (Fisher exact $p = 1 \times 10^{-20}$). No structural-confidence metric separated binders from non-binders consistently across panels, whereas the function-trained model's predicted pKd gave the highest ROC AUC in every panel, 0.79 to 0.92, and ranked measured affinity among function-guided binders at Spearman $ρ= 0.98$. On the design objective, Tb/Dy selectivity, the function-guided designs also exceeded the natural lanmodulin family, outranking a randomly drawn ortholog 84% of the time across 149 orthologs. Structural confidence is a plausibility signal, not a selection criterion for function; direct supervision on measured function is what ranks designs.

items.title: Symmetry-Induced Conservation Laws, Three-Channel Attribution, and Solid-Phase Recycling in Prebiotic Enantiomeric Excess Amplification
items.summary: Enantiomeric excess is the primary observable used to quantify chiral amplification across prebiotic chemistry, asymmetric autocatalysis, and multiphase crystallization. Because enantiomeric excess divides net chiral excess by total chiral mass, identical increases can arise either from parity-breaking synthesis of chiral centers or from symmetric phase and oligomer partitioning that depletes soluble mass. We establish a pathwise conservation law, a model-free three-channel attribution identity, and a continuous path-covariant Aumann--Shapley attribution for mirror-symmetric reaction networks. In any closed network lacking autocatalytic feedback or epimerization, net chiral excess remains invariant along every stochastic trajectory, locking liquid-phase amplification inversely to surviving chiral mass while Shear--Kramers--Lorentz relative-entropy balance bounds dissipation. We re-analyze seven experimental benchmark systems and show that standalone phase removal loses $91.7\%$--$98.9\%$ of chiral solute into racemic sediment in closed batches and washes out under open racemic inflow. We show that coupling eutectic partitioning with racemization recycling achieves $96.5\%$ homochiral crystal recovery, whereas evaporative autocatalysis crosses the open-flow bifurcation threshold with $81.9\%$ homochiral yield. Finally, we extend our non-crossing parity invariant across a fifty-nine-point multicomponent peptide ligation and seeded co-precipitation benchmark, evaluate a one-hundred-twelve-row calcite adsorption dataset, and resolve mineral-occlusion non-identifiability using three-block antipodal crystal pairs.

items.title: Counting doubly labelled trees and one-component networks
items.summary: A phylogenetic network is one-component if the child of every reticulation is a leaf. This class of networks has been widely used as building blocks in the combinatorial study of phylogenetic networks. We establish a bijection between one-component networks on $k$ taxa and rooted binary multi-labelled trees in which every label occurs exactly twice. Using this bijection and Burnside's lemma, we derive a closed formula and a two-term recurrence for the number of one-component networks. We further obtain explicit formulas for counting one-component networks with a prescribed number of reticulations.

items.title: Calibeating Prediction-Powered Inference
items.summary: We study semisupervised mean estimation with a small labeled sample, a large unlabeled sample, and a black-box prediction model whose output may be miscalibrated. A standard approach in this setting is augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) [Robins et al., 1994], which protects against prediction-model misspecification but may be inefficient when the prediction score is poorly aligned with the outcome scale. We introduce Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference, which post-hoc calibrates the prediction score on the labeled sample before using it for semisupervised estimation. This simple step requires no retraining and can calibeat the original score, improving it both as a predictor of the outcome and as a regression adjustment for semisupervised inference. We study both linear and isotonic calibration. For isotonic calibration, we establish first-order optimality guarantees: isotonic post-processing can improve predictive accuracy and estimator efficiency relative to the original score and simpler post-processing rules, while replacing the fitted isotonic score by its conditional-mean oracle yields no additional first-order variance reduction. For linear calibration, we show first-order equivalence to PPI++. We also clarify the relationship between existing estimators, showing that the original PPI estimator is a special case of AIPW and can be inefficient when the prediction model is accurate, while PPI++ is AIPW with empirical efficiency maximization [Rubin and van der Laan, 2008]. In simulations and real-data experiments, our calibrated estimators often outperform PPI and are competitive with, or outperform, AIPW and PPI++. We provide an accompanying Python package, ppi_aipw, at https://larsvanderlaan.github.io/ppi-aipw/.

items.title: Planning as Dynamics Relaxation: Hippocampal Recurrent Network Realizes Optimal Goal-Directed Navigation
items.summary: Neural correlates of the cognitive map are well documented, yet how a neural circuit turns a stored map into an obstacle-avoiding route remains unclear. Here we show that a hippocampal network with appropriate recurrent connections achieves optimal goal-directed navigation through its own relaxation dynamics. The recurrent weights represent the transition probabilities between the locations the neurons encode, walls are reflected by vanishing weights, and behavioral-timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP) writes this connectivity during goal-free exploration. When a goal is recalled, a top-down current clamps the goal neuron and the population relaxes into a goal-locked activity field. We prove that this field is the desirability field of a linearly-solvable Markov decision process: the relaxed state is the exact optimum of a stated control problem, the KL-regularized objective of Todorov, and the optimal next-step distribution is carried by the branch synaptic currents. The identity extends to directed transitions, and a weak-cost limit returns the Green's function of the recurrent Laplacian. A place-tuned readout converts the field's log-gradient into a direction of travel, and the same synapses answer a predictive query when the source is placed at the current location. Simulations on mazes with complex obstacles show near-shortest routes, an identity that survives a thousand-fold range of recall amplitude, the loss of 80% of place cells, and tens of thousands of states, low-rank updates of every plan after a local change, and a transient that is anytime: the local action is ready long before the field converges. We hope this offers a general circuit principle for planning in abstract cognitive maps beyond spatial navigation.

items.title: CupOFMoCA: Coupled Objective-Guided Discrete Flows for Molecular Conjugate Assembly
items.summary: Molecular conjugates, including PROTACs and peptide-drug conjugates (PDCs), derive their function from the joint behavior of multiple coupled components, yet most generative approaches design these components independently and combine them only after generation. Such staged pipelines ignore cross-component dependencies and often produce conjugates that are chemically invalid, fall outside empirical conjugate distributions, or lose function upon assembly. In this work, we introduce Coupled Objective-Guided Discrete Flows for Molecular Conjugate Assembly (CupOFMoCA), a discrete generative method that enforces cross-component chemical constraints during conjugate generation. CupOFMoCA restricts guided updates to chemically feasible conjugate states and reweights local transitions using molecular design objectives. Across three PDC systems, coupled generation achieved 100% conjugation validity among valid peptides and increased valid yield over matched post-hoc filtering, with comparable predicted binding scores across the full valid sets. In three-seed evaluations of three PROTAC systems, CupOFMoCA achieved the highest assembly validity on two systems and generated more assembly-valid molecules per second than the evaluated baselines. We further evaluated the generated PROTACs with post-hoc DegradeMaster scoring and explicit-solvent molecular dynamics, supporting their predicted activity and conformational properties. Together, these results establish CupOFMoCA as an efficient generator of molecular conjugates, supporting therapeutic development via coordinated control of assembly and molecular properties.

items.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
items.summary: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.

items.title: Subject-Held-Out Evaluation of Deep Ground Reaction Force Estimators Across Two Laboratories: Leakage and Cross-Laboratory Transfer
items.summary: Deep networks that estimate ground reaction forces and centers of pressure from motion-capture markers are validated within one laboratory, in a seldom-stated coordinate frame, and sometimes with trial-level splits that put the same person in the training and the test set. We measured what each practice costs, and whether such models transfer between laboratories. Three sequence models (convolutional, convolutional-recurrent, and convolutional-transformer) were evaluated on two independent datasets, locomotion (6 subjects) and occupational patient handling (10 subjects), under one pipeline, one tuning procedure, three seeds, and four protocols: trial-level split, leave-one-subject-out, pooled two-laboratory training with matched held-out subjects, and cross-laboratory transfer. At a fixed configuration, trial-level splits overstated the subject-held-out coefficient of determination by +0.040 to +0.194; on occupational data the overstatement exceeded every difference between architectures. With subjects held out, the three models reached values between 0.583 and 0.804; the leader differed between datasets, and gaps lay within subject-to-subject variability. Pooling the laboratories changed neither dataset on matched subjects. Transfer between laboratories was below chance in both directions, including the vertical force, which no in-plane rotation can affect. Leaving force targets in the plate frame while inputs were heading-aligned cost 0.57 of locomotion anteroposterior-force explained variance, enough to make that force look hardest; a Newton's-law correlation detected the mismatch before training. Split protocol and target frame changed reported accuracy more than architecture did. Learned force estimators should be validated with subjects held out, checked for frame consistency before training, and tested across laboratories before deployment claims are made.

items.title: PertReason: A Knowledge-Grounded Benchmark and Framework for Cell-State-Conditioned Mechanistic Reasoning of Perturbation Effects
items.summary: Evaluating machine learning in scientific domains requires separating correct predictions from correct reasons under realistic distribution shifts. We introduce PertReason, a knowledge-grounded approach to evaluating and improving cell-state-conditioned reasoning about perturbation effects. Our framework comprises PertReasonQA, a benchmark that provides evaluation and supervision, and PertReasonLM, a reference large language model that demonstrates how such supervision supports reasoning-centric training. PertReasonQA tests whether models can generate mechanistically faithful explanations while remaining robust to complex shifts, such as new cells, unseen perturbations, cross-modal or combinatorial extrapolations. PertReasonQA combines single-cell genetic and chemical perturbation data across multiple cellular contexts with knowledge graphs, and dynamically conditions pathways on cell-specific basal states to avoid generic memorization. Evaluations of state-of-the-art models reveal systematic gaps between outcome prediction and mechanistic reasoning. As a reference probe of the benchmark, PertReasonLM is trained through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning using mechanistic supervision from PertReasonQA. PertReasonLM improves predictive accuracy and reduces answer-reason disagreement by grounding rationales in context-specific pathways. Together, we provide a diagnostic framework for exposing and mitigating failures in faithful reasoning in data-rich scientific systems. We release our datasets to support further research at https://dongkwan-kim.github.io/PertReason/.

items.title: Silscore: modelling siRNA potency with positional thermodynamics and data-selected nucleotide-identity terms
items.summary: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) enable programmable gene silencing, but candidates targeting the same transcript can differ markedly in potency. Existing predictors range from interpretable empirical rules with limited accuracy to high-capacity models that can lose performance when datasets or targets change. We present Silscore, a guide-only model that combines a quadratic preference for overall duplex stability, a position-resolved profile of nearest-neighbour stacking energies and sparse nucleotide-identity terms selected from residuals left unexplained by thermodynamics. Its main fit uses 26 parameters, fewer than half as many as any trainable comparator evaluated here. We evaluate Silscore on the canonical split of the Huesken dataset, two external datasets (Mixset and Katoh-Suzuki), and an evaluation in which the same guides are tested after training on dissimilar targets. Silscore attains the highest observed Pearson correlation in all three transfer evaluations, and the data support an advantage over every applicable comparator on Katoh-Suzuki. For a fixed evaluation set, we compare two equally sized training sets with higher or lower sequence similarity to the evaluation sequences. After training on the less similar sequences, Silscore has the highest observed correlation, and the data do not establish a change in its performance. The fitted parameters can also be interpreted directly: identity terms locate sequence effects that base-pairing energies cannot express, global stability has a data-estimated intermediate optimum, and local energy profiles recover terminal asymmetry and a preference for weaker seed and stronger central pairing. Silscore thus provides a compact, data-driven model that combines strong predictive performance with robustness when tested in new settings and expresses previously reported empirical preferences as quantities estimated from data.

items.title: PDO Drug Screening Data for Evaluating and Training AI Drug Response Prediction Models
items.summary: Anti-cancer drug response prediction (DRP) is critically important for precision oncology and therapeutic development. Currently, most DRP models are developed using drug screening data from immortalized cancer cell lines, which can differ substantially from patient tumors at the genomic and molecular levels, even though patient tumor response is the ultimate prediction target. To help bridge this gap and bring DRP models closer to their intended clinical application, we conducted four drug screening studies using patient-derived organoids (PDOs), which more faithfully recapitulate patient tumors than immortalized cell lines. These studies generated data for improving and evaluating DRP models, including multi-omics profiles of PDO lines, drug feature data, and treatment response measurements. Using these data, we retrained and evaluated multiple publicly available DRP models under three model-building scenarios: training models using cell line data only, training models using combined cell line and PDO data, and pretraining models on cell line data followed by fine-tuning on PDO data. We then evaluated and compared model prediction performance on PDOs across these analysis scenarios. In addition, we also assessed the consistency of drug screening viability data generated by different laboratories using different assay technologies and/or experimental protocols.

items.title: Robot-Induced Bias in Movement Smoothness Metrics for Rehabilitation: Quantification and Correction in Simulation
items.summary: Robot mechanics can bias kinematic measures of recovery and limit comparisons across rehabilitation devices. We developed a closed-loop human-robot simulation calibrated to published healthy and stroke group kinematics. Paired runs held motor-control parameters and movement plans fixed to quantify bias in seven metrics relative to a low-impedance reference, normalized using external repeatability benchmarks. Within a subset informed by published device specifications, median log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) bias was 0.93 and 1.79 benchmark units for stroke and healthy profiles, respectively. Sobol analysis identified Coulomb friction and apparent mass as leading contributors; LDLJ bias persisted across 11 robustness variants. LDLJ bias increased as simulated movements became less fragmented. If recovery similarly reduces fragmentation, this effect could partly mask improvement in measured smoothness. Correction combining identified robot dynamics and observed metrics with gradient-boosted trees reduced median normalized absolute error from 0.77 to 0.10 for LDLJ and from 0.24 to 0.08 for spectral arc length (SPARC) in the device-informed subset of a random 20% hold-out. Median smoothness residuals remained at or below 0.15 benchmark units across four separately held-out parameter regions. Under an alternative controller, LDLJ error decreased from 1.60 to 0.17 without retraining, although transfer varied across metrics. These simulation results support mechanical characterization and movement-dependent correction toward more comparable robotic assessments, motivating validation in patients.

items.title: Designing Cell-Type-Specific Regulatory DNA with Guided Discrete Diffusion
items.summary: AI-driven design of DNA with cell-type-specific regulatory activity is broadly relevant for cell engineering and gene therapy. DNA elements such as promoters and enhancers have gene-regulatory functions that are defined by their DNA sequence and follow a characteristic regulatory grammar. Deep learning models can effectively predict DNA regulatory activity across cell types, but current generative methods often produce DNA sequences that deviate from the native regulatory grammar, increasing the risk of unexpected behavior and off-target effects in real-world applications. Here, we introduce DNA-CRAFT, a method for designing regulatory DNA with high predicted cell-type-specific activity while preserving naturalness. DNA-CRAFT formulates regulatory sequence design as a guided search over a generative model pre-trained on millions of naturally occurring regulatory elements from the human and mouse genomes. Our method enables targeted exploration of the DNA sequence space, efficient evaluation of candidate designs, and explicit suppression of unwanted activity. Across benchmarks spanning human cell lines and primary immune cells, DNA-CRAFT combines high predicted cell-type specificity with strong motif and sequence-composition adherence, achieving favorable results across the evaluated DNA design tasks.

items.title: The Platonic brain bridge hypothesis: brain networks as architectural priors for multimodal large language models
items.summary: Multimodal large language models predict brain activity, but alignment has remained a measurement, not a design tool. We propose the Platonic brain bridge hypothesis: omni models, which jointly process video, audio and text, share brain-like representations usable in both directions. From model to brain, seven omni models show stable brain-likeness across participants, and our encoding experts lead the Algonauts 2025 out-of-distribution leaderboard by mean score. From brain to model, we make three contributions. Brain-MoE ties the experts of a frozen model to the seven cortical networks, raises held-out accuracy in all 15 model-benchmark pairs and exceeds capacity-matched random experts in 14. Brain-AVQA, to our knowledge the first audiovisual benchmark with cortical-network labels for every question, supplies the pretraining questions. Brain-Scope finds sparse features that predict brain responses, steer routing and, when removed, weaken brain prediction. Human brain organization is therefore a usable architectural prior for multimodal large language models.

items.title: A disease-contextualized atlas of proteome-scale molecular influences of natural products
items.summary: Understanding the system-wide molecular effects of natural products remains challenging because chemical knowledge is fragmented, proteomic coverage is incomplete, and experimental perturbation data are scarce, particularly for multicomponent medicinal herbs. Here we present an integrative framework for modeling molecular influences of natural compounds and medicinal herbs in disease-specific contexts. We harmonized three herbal medicine databases to establish a standardized atlas of 46,422 chemical entities, 12,459 medicinal herbs, and 156,588 herb-compound associations. We integrated high-confidence protein-protein interactions with proteomic and transcriptomic data to reconstruct molecular networks across nine cancers. By prioritizing protein-level evidence and using transcriptomic associations to extend coverage, these networks capture disease-associated interaction rewiring beyond differential expression. We coupled AI-inferred compound-target interactions with signed random walks with restart to model the propagation of molecular influences from sparse direct targets to directional, genome-scale network profiles. Using gastric cancer as an in-depth case study, we generated profiles for 45,418 compounds across 16,899 molecular nodes and explored multicomponent herbal interventions. We further applied the framework to eight additional cancers and retrospectively compared selected profiles with published drug-perturbation proteomics. This atlas provides a scalable basis for systems-level modeling of natural-product interventions and mechanism-guided drug discovery.

items.title: Optogenetic Modulation Fraction: A Robust Opsin-Presence Effect and an Unresolved Cell-Type Question, by Censoring-Aware Survival Analysis of Public Neuropixels Data
items.summary: Expressing channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) in an interneuron population substantially raises the fraction of locally recorded units whose spike timing is altered by light, relative to no-opsin controls, under every method tried. Establishing that result rigorously, and retracting two secondary claims that did not survive the same rigor, is this paper's actual content. We reanalyze eight public Allen Institute Neuropixels sessions (4,112 units), modeling light-to-first-spike latency as a right-censored time-to-event outcome, with a Cox model, pooled FDR correction, and a small-cluster-robust test (logistic regression plus an exact wild cluster bootstrap, since only eight session clusters exist). We report an unrestricted modulation fraction and a restricted direct-responder fraction (evoked latency under 10 ms, an explicit, literature-grounded threshold). ChR2-expressing Sst/Pvalb sessions show a large, bootstrap-confirmed elevation over control under both metrics. Two further claims, each initially suggested by a standard test, did not survive the exact bootstrap or a direct formal check, and we report both retractions as results in their own right. Vip-ChR2's apparent elevation over control is not confirmed by the bootstrap and becomes non-significant once restricted to direct responders. A second pattern, that among modulated units Vip sessions had a higher proportion of direct responses than Sst/Pvalb, opposite the raw ordering, evaporated under the same bootstrap test: no genotype contrast approaches significance, and control has the highest proportion of all three, which cannot be biological. Per-session rates vary enormously within one genotype. With two earlier corrections (a session-composition artifact and a standard-versus-exact-bootstrap discrepancy), this is a four-correction paper: pooled estimates and secondary patterns deserve the same scrutiny as a headline claim.

items.title: Lilith: Developmental Modular LLMs with Chemical Signaling
items.summary: Current paradigms in Artificial Intelligence rely on layers of feedforward networks which model brain activity at the neuronal level. We conjecture that expanding to the level of multiple brain regions with chemical signaling may be a productive step toward understanding the emergence of consciousness. We propose LILITH, a novel architecture that combines developmental training of modular language models with brain-inspired token-based communication protocols, mirroring chemical signaling in the brain. Our approach models distinct brain regions as specialized LLM modules including thinking, memory, sensory, and regulatory components that communicate through emergent token-based signaling protocols analogous to neurotransmitter networks. Unlike traditional pre-trained systems, LILITH would employ developmental training where untrained LLM architectures learn through simulated life experiences, developing communication pathways and cognitive abilities through environmental interaction and evolutionary optimization. This framework would enable direct empirical investigation of consciousness emergence using Integrated Information Theory metrics while providing unprecedented insight into inter-module signaling patterns during development. By optimizing for consciousness emergence rather than task performance, LILITH could provide insight into different emergent phenomena at multiple levels of neural correlates, contrasting neuronal-level processing with multi-region coordination dynamics. The goal of this paper is to put the idea forward while recognizing the substantial challenges in implementing such a system.

items.title: ADZE 2.0: rarefaction estimates of allelic richness and private allelic richness for whole-genome data
items.summary: Allelic richness and private allelic richness describe how alleles are distributed across populations, but both depend strongly on sample size. Rarefaction makes them comparable by computing the expected number of alleles in subsamples of a common size, and ADZE implemented this approach and an extension to alleles shared only by a set of populations. However, ADZE was developed for microsatellite data and cannot read sequencing data in variant call format (VCF). Here we present ADZE 2.0, which reads VCF, computes each statistic genome-wide or in genomic windows, and can treat blocks of phased SNPs as haplotype alleles. We also implement improved memory handling and multi-threading support. ADZE 2.0 reproduces the ADZE 1.0 estimates for human microsatellite data exactly. On chromosome 22 of the high-coverage 1000 Genomes Project data, private allelic richness for all 325 population pairs took 4.4 minutes on 32 threads. ADZE 2.0 is available at https://github.com/szpiech/ADZE.

items.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)
items.summary: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite broad potential impact of selection bias it is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct selection bias, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle, applicability, limitations and data requirements. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R and prepares input for the external SPREG software. It provides worked examples using simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with open methodological challenges.

items.title: Analysis choices decide whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1: a multiverse analysis of model-brain RSA
items.summary: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival trained networks as models of visual cortex, and we had reported an untrained-network advantage over backpropagation at V1 in THINGS fMRI, together with a dependence on evaluation resolution. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the untrained network scored below the trained one at every pooling grid (median r difference -0.043 at g = 4, 0 of 5 seeds positive), and also in MSE skill and per-fold r. In exploratory analyses, across 36 combinations of unit normalisation, distance measure and voxel normalisation (28 distinct analyses), the sign of the V1 contrast depended on the analysis (intervals above 0 in 5 and below 0 in 9 distinct analyses), and in our networks the resolution dependence of the original convention appeared in only one cell. Raw correlation-distance representational similarity analysis (RSA) covaried with the alignment of model and voxel patterns with the unit-mean profile (Spearman 0.97 across our networks, 0.79 across six ImageNet architectures); the advantage was absent from the component orthogonal to the mean profile, and the parallel component alone did not resolve it. On the unweighted angular component of centred patterns, trained networks were ahead at V1 (our network and 5 of 6 ImageNet models) and at LOC (all seven); the norm-weighted angular term was not resolved. A luminance-and-contrast bank scored above every network under ridge (point estimates), and adding network features under a shared penalty did not improve prediction. Intervals are stimulus-bootstrap intervals for three subjects, and 6 pre-stated predictions were not met. We recommend reporting sensitivity to centring over the evaluated stimuli on both sides, reporting components separately, and including a small multiverse and simple baselines.

items.title: Uncertainty-aware integration of deuterium metabolic imaging with genome-scale metabolic modeling reveals diet-associated feasible-space remodeling in mouse skeletal muscle
items.summary: Deuterium metabolic imaging (DMI) measures glucose-derived labeling in vivo, but noisy time courses complicate network-level interpretation. We developed an uncertainty-aware workflow that integrates dynamic DMI data with genome-scale metabolic modeling (GEM) through soft flux constraints. After injection of [6,6'-2H2]glucose, dynamic spectra were acquired from gastrocnemius, soleus, and tibialis anterior muscles of control and high-fat diet (HFD) mice. A hierarchical four-state kinetic model estimated labeling parameters while accounting for shared plasma input, tissue-specific kinetics, voxel-level fluxes, isotope effects, and measurement uncertainty. Because glucose labeling was more reliable than lactate and glutamate/glutamine signals, only two DMI-derived quantities were used as GEM anchors: glucose processing mapped to hexokinase flux, and glucose-derived oxidative entry mapped to mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase flux. Two-sided soft target intervals with weighted penalties defined DMI-compatible feasible regions for each mouse and muscle. Flux variability analysis and sampling assessed changes across reactions and metabolic subsystems. The constraints were compatible with the muscle network and affected feasible activity in glycolysis, lactate metabolism, pyruvate oxidation, the TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and redox pathways. HFD-associated changes differed by muscle: tibialis anterior and soleus showed reduced glucose-linked feasible activity, whereas gastrocnemius showed mixed changes with preserved or increased TCA and redox activity.
